issues.title: Identity Assertion Authz Grant allows broadening the scope
issues.author: obfuscoder
issues.body:
I followed the presentation at the IETF 119 for this topic. The profile describes how an ID Token is used to get a JWT Authorization Grant and then to get an Access Token for that JWT Authorization Grant. The scope can be defined by the client when requesting the access token.

As the JWT Authorization Grant profile is designed to allow interop across several domains, each AS in the participating domain will support creating authorization grant JWTs as well as accepting authorization grant JWTs to issue access tokens.

Usually a client receives an access token alongside the ID Token and the client can use Token Exchange to get additional access tokens with equal or narrowed down scope.

The ID Token does not contain any scope. So even if a client only received an Access Token with a specific narrow scope, the client could abuse this grant by asking AS of domain A for an authorization grant JWT based on the Id Token and then use this authz grant JWT at the AS of domain A again to obtain a new access token with arbitrary scope (up to what is allowed for the client as per policy).

Although this could be prohibited by the AS not accepting authorization grant JWTs it issued itself, the client could request the authorization grant JWT from the AS of domain B with just a couple more steps.

Granted, this may not be relevant for the enterprise environment the JWT authorization grant profile is meant for as the End-User is usually not asked for giving consent to the scope requested by clients and instead the allowed scope in defined by policies within the AS configs. However, I'd like to ask if this is something worth to consider.

issues.title: Why don't the IdP requests the access token from the AS?
issues.author: randomstuff

comments.author: kamronbatman
comments.body:
The approach we took (which is malleable, as we want to build a simple and reusable flow with the least assumptions), is to have the least amount of burden on both the client (requesting application) and the RS AS. In doing that,  step 3 is fine because right now clients already are registered with the RS AS to request tokens directly and facilitate SSO flows. We wanted to lean into that by shifting as much of the burden to the identity provider, especially since the identity provider has all of the information about the user/organization and their relationships.

I do like the simplicity of the proposed modified scenario and I think we should continue hammering out details to see if this kind of approach could work.

I think we also agree that front loading the `client_id` and `resource` identifiers for mapping on the identity provider is not ideal. Unfortunately, I also believe requiring the IdP to register a client on every RS AS to do a new on-behalf exchange is not ideal either, especially since that is technically 3rd party to the existing client and AS oAuth registration/trust relationship.

comments.author: randomstuff
comments.body:
So I've been thinking (more/better) about my modified scenario. Some drawbacks are:

* If a refresh_token was issued, the IdP now would be responsible for handling the token refresh request and forwarding it to the AS. I guess the IdP would have to store the original refresh token and send a new refresh token to the client.
* The IdP would now be responsible for handling token revocations requests from the client. For the refresh token, the the approach from the previous point could be used but this is more complex for the access token.
* The IdP would have to forward (and possibly filter/translate) many parameters such as scope, etc.
* The client would not have the AS server metadata as it would not have a direct relationship with the AS.
* DPoP forwarding would not work.

comments.author: sdesen
comments.body:
If all AS responsibilities required for a typical OAuth consent flow were shifted to the IdP, then the IdP would become the AS for an intents and purposes, and then the Client would just make a typical request for an access token. No other steps would be needed. This spec is intended to leverage the common scenario where OAuth relationships exist and the AS may be independent of the IdP.

However, I agree it makes sense to think about where changes can be made for the scenario where the relationship might not already exist, so very much appreciate this comment.

For this point:
> the client does not need to know that the RS is associated with another domain;

I am not sure I understand if this is true, because the client needs to make the resource request regardless from the RS.

issues.title: Discuss the need for client_id mapping
issues.author: randomstuff

Section 5.3 [Identity Assertion Authorization Grant JWT](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-parecki-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant#name-identity-assertion-authoriz) says that the IdP should generate a Identity Assertion Authorization Grant JWT with:

> client_id - Client ID as registered with the Resource Application's authorization server

issues.title: Add Authorization Server metadata to enable discovery of grant/token type.
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
[OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8414) enables a client to discover capabilities of a given authorization server.   For example a client can fetch AS metadata to determine what endpoints, grant types, and scopes the AS supports and then dynamically construct a valid request for a supported granted type.  This enables the client to negotiate the right capabilities at runtime with an Authorization Server vs hard-coding assumptions for a given AS.

A given client currently as no mechanism to discover

- Whether an AS supports issuing `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag` token type with Token Exchange
- Whether an AS supports `oauth-id-jag+jwt` JWT as a valid JWT bearer grant type (`urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer`)

Unfortunately [Token Exchange](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693)  doesn't define an authorization server metadata parameter for `requested_token_types_supported`  that could publish `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag` as supported token type.  Adding the registration would enable clients to discover what token types they could request from a given AS

Similarly, the new draft revision of [JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-jones-oauth-rfc7523bis-00.html)  also doesn't define an authorization server metadata parameter for what profiles are supported.  A new parameter such as `jwt_assertion_token_types_supported` would enable a client to know what assertion profiles an Authorization Supports such as `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag`. 

Without these additional values a client would need to hard-code support for this profile for a given Authorization Server.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
We need to treat these two questions separately. 

The question of whether an AS (IdP) supports the "ID JAG" token exchange is necessary to avoid hard-coding support for this with out-of-band information.

The question of whether the JWT bearer grant type is supported is less helpful, because we actually need more information than that to do anything useful. The main feedback we've heard from implementers is they want to know whether an access token request will work with this flow for a given user. That is more than just whether the grant type is supported at the AS, because it also depends on the policies configured at the IdP. So what's actually needed is more of a "list the applications I'll be able to get an access token using an ID-JAG from given the user and application context", which looks more like a service call and less like a static discovery document.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body: This PR on the Identity Chaining draft establishes the new `identity_chaining_requested_token_types_supported` property in AS metadata. I added a section to this draft for it. We'll address the second question about the JWT Bearer grant type later.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body: Closing this in favor of discussing the specifics of the JWT Assertion Grant discovery question in #34

issues.title: Client ID Registration
issues.author: PieterKas
issues.body:
"client_id: : REQUIRED - An identifier of the client that this JWT was issued to, which MUST be recognized by the Resource Application's authorization server. For interoperability, the client identifier SHOULD be a client_id as defined in Section 4.3 {{RFC8693}}."

Is the expectation for this draft that the same client_id is used and registered with different authorisation servers in different domains (in this case the IdP and Resource Application Authorization Server? This might get unwieldy at scale, especially in a world where a client may have to register with multiple authorisation servers.

As an alternative, some allowance for supporting multiple client_ids might be needed. This may be either through some kind of static mapping (also hard to maintain), or by allowing the client to specify additional client_ids for which the assertion may be used. 

An additional point to clarify may be that the Resource Appliction's Authorization Server MUST verifiy that the client_id in the assertion match the client_id of the client presenting the assertion.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
No, there is no expectation that everyone shares the same client ID database, that's why I used the language "recognized by the Resource Application's authorization server".

I hadn't considered multiple, that could be an option.

comments.author: PieterKas
comments.body:
>No, there is no expectation that everyone shares the same client ID database, that's why I used the language "recognized by the Resource Application's authorization server".

So, if I had a client that was registered with the IdP, and I used client_id_1 for that, I would not be expected to also use client_id_1 with the Resource applications authorization server, but could use client_id_2 with the Resource application's authorization server. How would the IdP know client_id_2 when including it in the JWT Authorization grant? There should probably be some guidance on implementation options (including a protocol option to allow the client to define what it wants as the client_id in the JWT - along with security considerations on that practice).

issues.title: Nits in the draft
issues.author: deansaxe
issues.body:
After reviewing the draft and discussing with @aaronpk last week, I have two nits to discuss to help clarify the language in the doc:

Section 5.2 under **scope** states, "This may be fewer scopes than the application requested".  I believe the intent is that the scopes cannot grow in their impact.  This may be fewer in number, or it may be more scopes with a narrower set of authorized actions.  I suggest rewriting this slightly to clarify the intent is to constrain the scope, not the number of scopes in use.

Section 7.3 states, "The Identity Providers SHOULD NOT issue access tokens in response to an ID-JAG it issued itself".  I agree with the intent, but stronger language is necessary.  I suggest changing this to "MUST NOT".

issues.title: Change the `resource` param in the token exchange request to identify the RS
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
**Assumptions:**

* Authorization Servers identify Resource Servers with globally unique URIs

**Solution:**

Change the definition of the `resource` parameter to identify the resource server that the final access token will be used at. 

```
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&resource=https://api.example.com/
&scope=read
&subject_token=eyJraWQiOiJzMTZ0cVNtODhwREo4VGZCXzdrSEtQ...
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
&client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIyIn0...
```

**Notes:**

* The IdP would need to be able to uniquely identify the resource identifier, and know which authorization server is used by that resource server. The IdP could include both the AS issuer and RS identifier in the ID Assertion JWT.
* This requires that resource identifiers are globally unique, and the IdP will need to validate that the developer of the app controls the URL, to avoid a random person from using `https://google.com/` as their resource identifier.
* Not everyone actually uses resource identifiers or has multiple resources under an AS, so it's not clear what value to use in those cases. Just the AS issuer identifier?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
> The IdP would need to be able to uniquely identify the resource identifier, and know which authorization server is used by that resource server

If we assume an ID Assertion Grant only supports a single issuer (aka authorization server) that has 0 or more resources then we could support multiple `resource` params in the request where at least 1 param value must the issuer.  This would address your last point of "Not everyone actually uses resource identifiers or has multiple resources under an AS, so it's not clear what value to use in those cases. Just the AS issuer identifier?"

> This requires that resource identifiers are globally unique, and the IdP will need to validate that the developer of the app controls the URL, to avoid a random person from using https://google.com/ as their resource identifier

Again if we assume a single issuer is supported, then only the issuer's `resource` value would have to be unique. The IdP would resolve additional resources using the issuer as the key. _Note the non-issuer value just needs to be a URI not a URL_

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Both this approach and #24 have the same challenge with `resource` or `audience` being  "where the client intends to use the requested security token".   The ID Assertion Grant is not an access token so it must first be exchanged for an access token but still needs to capture the authorization needed for an access token.     Since we are defining a new token type with its own semantics, I'm OK with this ambiguity as the end-result is authorization the requested resource.

comments.author: sdesen
comments.body: The language there indicates "target service" which could be a combined application of the authorization server and resource server. The current implemented treats scopes as the scopes used for the eventual resource server token, further blurring the lines.

issues.title: Use `audience` to identify the AS and `resource` to identify the RS
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Token Exchange defines `resource` as a URI and `audience` as a string.

We could use `audience` to identify the AS issuer URL, and `resource` to identify the resource server.

```
POST /oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Host: acme.idp.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&audience=https://auth.example.com/
&resource=https://acme.chat.example/
&scope=chat.read+chat.history
&subject_token=eyJraWQiOiJzMTZ0cVNtODhwREo4VGZCXzdrSEtQ...
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
&client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIyIn0...
```

**Notes:**

* This maps most cleanly to Resource Indicators (RFC8707)
* This slightly violates the meaning of the `audience` and `resource` parameters in Token Exchange, since Token Exchange says that the client is asking for a token usable at all the requested target services.
* For services that don't have a resource identifier, the `resource` parameter could be omitted without it being weird.

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
> This slightly violates the meaning of the audience and resource parameters in Token Exchange, since Token Exchange says that the client is asking for a token usable at all the requested target services.

I believe we could squint a bit here knowing that what Token Exchange issues here is `requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag`, i.e. not an actual access token.

The result of this being the following assertion

```
{
  "typ": "oauth-id-jag+jwt"
}
.
{
  "jti": "9e43f81b64a33f20116179",
  "iss": "https://acme.idp.example",
  "sub": "U019488227",
  "aud": "https://auth.example.com/",
  "resource": "https://acme.chat.example/", // or "resource": ["resource1", "resource2", ...n] when multiple resource parameters are used
  "client_id": "f53f191f9311af35",
  "exp": 1311281970,
  "iat": 1311280970,
  "scope": "chat.read chat.history"
}
.
signature
```

I think this is OK and most expressive of the three #22 linked threads.

issues.title: Use multiple `resource` parameters, the Authorization Server issuer and one or more Resource Server identifiers
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Token Exchange allows parameters to be repeated, so we could pass multiple `resource` parameters.

```
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&resource=https://auth.example.com/
&resource=https://api.example.com/
&scope=read
&subject_token=eyJraWQiOiJzMTZ0cVNtODhwREo4VGZCXzdrSEtQ...
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
&client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIyIn0...
```

Notes:

* This is the cleanest option for what to do if there is no Resource Server indicator needed, since the request would contain only one value, the Authorization Server issuer identifier
* Repeated parameters in form-encoded requests have a bit of a messy history, not every server framework supports them the same way. Some ignore repeated values, some require adding `[]` to indicate repeated values.

issues.title: Proof-of-Possession Token for Resource App
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
The spec currently isn't clear how a client should meet proof-of-possesion requirements such as DPOP for an ID-JAG for Resource App's Authorization Server token request or the issued token from a Resource App's Authorization Server for a Resource App's Resource Server

OAuth Identity and Authorization Chaining Across Domains has a section on [Delegated Key Binding](https://drafts.oauth.net/oauth-identity-chaining/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining.html#name-delegated-key-binding)

ID Assertions currently don't support proof-of-possesion although some folks [have found workarounds](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey)

Since `actor_token` is not used by this profile, we currently don't flow any `cnf` claims into the ID-JAG.  

- Should the client just send a DPoP proof JWT in a DPoP header when making an access token request to the Resource App's Authorization Server?   
  - A client is currently free to use a different key with each Resource App Authorization Server as there is not binding back to the ID-JAG
- Should we also support a DPoP proof with ID-JAG? 
  - A client can pass the proof on the token exchange request and we could flow to the ID-JAG and the Resource App Authorization Server could verify the proof. 



I think it should be possible to bind a ID-JAG to a key

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
> I think it should be possible to bind a ID-JAG to a key

I think so too.

- Proof of possession presented during Token Exchange -> ID-JAG gets a `cnf` as per [RFC7800](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7800.html) _/ [DPoP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html). /but there's no indication in the response that binding was done tho (token_type is fixed to N_A), does it matter? I think not, the client can simply do PoP again during ID-JAG exchange/_
- Proof of possession presented during ID-JAG exchange
	- (ID-JAG has cnf) - it must match and tokens get constrained, failure otherwise
	- (ID-JAG doesn't have cnf) - tokens get constrained
- Proof of possession not presented during ID-JAG exchange
	- (ID-JAG has cnf) - failure
	- (ID-JAG doesn't have cnf) - tokens are not constrained or error (if RS is configured to require constrained tokens)

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Since the client needs to send the DPoP proof in a header for a token request with sender-constrained ID-JAG for the Resource App's AS, its not clear that the client is also requesting that the issued access token is also sender-constrained.  The DPoP proof is needed to validate the ID-JAG but also indicates desire to key bind the access token with RFC 9449.   

The simple answer is that if the ID-JAG contains a `cnf` claim then the issued access token is also bound to the same `cnf` when the AS supports issuing sender-constrained access token for the audience.   A client can't use a different key and can't opt-out of sender-constraining an access token for Resource App if they presented a sender-constrained ID-JAG and the Resource App supports sender-constrained access tokens for the Resource Apps' audience.  Thoughts?

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
It's the AS decision whether to issue a sender-constrained token for a particular RS or not, that depends on the configuration at or discretion of the AS. A client sending a proof of possession to the call is but a prerequisite to the decision process.

> https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html#section-5-9
> An authorization server MAY elect to issue access tokens that are not DPoP bound, which is signaled to the client with a value of Bearer in the token_type parameter of the access token response

So to update the earlier post

- Proof of possession presented during Token Exchange -> ID-JAG gets a `cnf` as per [RFC7800](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7800.html) _/ [DPoP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html). /but there's no indication in the response that binding was done tho (token_type is fixed to N_A), does it matter? I think not, the client can simply do PoP again during ID-JAG exchange/_
- Proof of possession presented during ID-JAG exchange
	- (ID-JAG has cnf) - it must match and tokens may get constrained per the RS configuration at the AS, failure otherwise
	- (ID-JAG doesn't have cnf) - tokens may get constrained per the RS configuration at the AS
- Proof of possession not presented during ID-JAG exchange
	- (ID-JAG has cnf) - failure
	- (ID-JAG doesn't have cnf) - tokens are not constrained or error (if RS configuration at the AS is to require constrained tokens for that RS)

issues.title: Refresh tokens
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
There are two places where refresh tokens might come into the picture:

* The Token Exchange request (use an ID Token to get an ID-JAG)
* The Access Token request (use an ID-JAG to get an access token)

We should have some guidance or security considerations around the implications of returning refresh tokens for both of these.

## IDP refresh tokens

The implication of returning a refresh token along with the ID-JAG is that the requesting application could use the refresh token in place of the ID token in future requests. This could allow the IDP to return new ID-JAGs without a new ID token having been requested.

## Resource App refresh tokens

The resource app could return a refresh token along with the access token. This pattern should be discouraged, as this enables the client to request access tokens in the future which the IDP wouldn't know about.

comments.author: joshcanhelp
comments.body: I've had some time to think about this and just wanted to add a few comments and thoughts on this. For the first option, **IDP refresh tokens**, there could be a refresh token returned with the initial ID token (green text appended to the diagram on the MCP PR): To refresh the service's access token, the MCP Client ("Client" going forward) would: 1. Use the refresh token with the IDP to get a new ID token 2. Use that ID token with the IDP to get a new ID JAG 3. ... continues as previously described That would allow the IDP to stay in the loop and invalidate the refresh process as needed (admin action, automated protection, etc). That would end up being 3 HTTP requests for a single refresh, though, which is a lot in the case of access tokens with a short life. For the second, **Resource App refresh tokens**, you said that the Client could request access tokens that the IDP wouldn't know about but the IDP would know that refresh tokens were allowed. Section 5 (page 8) of the "Identity Assertion Authorization Grant" document talks about the token exchange request and includes API scopes as a part of that request. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-parecki-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/ The `offline_access` scope could be requested there and then the IDP would know that refresh tokens are being requested. It could not control the refresh process, of course, so it makes sense to caution about that approach. That leads me to a question here in the context of this being applied to 3rd party APIs: how can the IDP be aware of the scopes being requested, `offline_access` or otherwise? I don't see that property mentioned in [your blog post](https://aaronparecki.com/2025/05/12/27/enterprise-ready-mcp) and can't really think of a great way for the IDP to get that knowledge and keep it up to date. One thing that came to mind is maybe the 3rd party URL could present a consent screen with all allowed scopes as selectable. Claude can get a text response with an URL and present it to a user and this type of interaction looks like it will be more formalized in the spec going forward (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/887). Thanks again for your work in this space!

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
This was resolved in the Identity Chaining Issue https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-chaining/pull/151#discussion_r2084222098

1. Client should request `offline_access` scope from IdP and obtain a refresh token
2. Client should use the IdP refresh token to obtain a new ID Token
3. Client should use a non-expired ID Token to Token Exchange for an ID-JAG
4. Client should only obtain an access token from the Resource App Authorization Server. The Resource App AS should never issue a Refresh Token for an ID-JAG

I wanted profiles like ID-JAG to make their own assessment on whether the Resource App AS can issue a Refresh Token (e.g Enterprise has a valid revocation mechanism such as CAEP/SSF) but this was overruled.

issues.title: Support for Multi-Instance Apps
issues.author: dlozlla
issues.body:
**Summary**
This proposal considers a protocol-level solution for scenarios where a user needs to connect to a specific instance (e.g., tenant, organziation, workspace) of a Resource App, particularly when these multiple instances share a common issuer URL. The goal is to create a mechanism that allows a Requesting App to specify the target instance and ensures this choice is communicated end-to-end, so it can be correctly interpreted by both the IdP and the Resource App's authorization server.

**Problem**
In many enterprise environments, a single application may offer multiple distinct instances. For example, consider an observability platform with separate instances for `development` and `production` logs. Often, these instances share a single `audience` (i.e., issuer URL) and `resource` identifier for their APIs. In these cases, access to the Resource App's API is managed by a custom claim injected into the `access_token` after the user authenticates with a specific instance.

The current Identity Assertion Authorization Grant does not define a standard way for a Requesting App to specify a target instance under these conditions. This ambiguity prevents a seamless user experience, which should ideally mirror selecting an application from an SSO dashboard and being directed to the correct instance.

This overall challenge can be broken down into two parts:

**1. The Discovery Problem** 
Before a user can make a choice, the Requesting App must first know what choices are available. How can the Requesting App learn which Resource Apps, and their specific instances, the logged-in user is permitted to connect to?

While solving discovery is critical for the end-to-end experience, it is handled separately in issue https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/issues/52. For this issue, we will assume the Requesting App has a method to determine which instance the user wants to access.

**2. The Request Problem** 
This is the focus of the proposal. Once the user has selected an instance, how does the Requesting App communicate this choice to the IdP? The current protocol lacks a standard parameter to differentiate the target instance when it shares an `audience`/issuer URL with others.

**Proposal**
**We propose using the `client_id` of the target Resource App instance within the IdP** as the unique identifier. This `client_id` would be included in the initial Token Exchange request and the resulting Identity Assertion (ID-JAG).

Rationale:
- Uniqueness & Existing Trust: Each Resource App instance registered with the IdP for SSO already has a unique `client_id`. This identifier is known and trusted by both the IdP and the Resource App.
- IdP Policy Enforcement: The IdP can use the provided `client_id` to locate and apply the specific authorization policies associated with that instance.
- Resource App Tenant Mapping: The Resource App's Authorization Server already relies on this `client_id` for its OIDC federation with the IdP. It can therefore use the `client_id` from the assertion to unambiguously map the request to the correct internal tenant, organization, or workspace.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Clarifying some assumptions and relationships to open issues first
 
- There are multi-tenant (e.g. Google) and single-tenant IdPs (e.g Okta) that are the ID-JAG issuer
- There are multi-tenant and single-tenant RPs that are the ID-JAG audience
- Both the ID-JAG issuer and audience could support per-tenant clients or global (cross-tenant) clients.  

Tenancy is relevant from both an issuer and audience perspective

I opened #39 with intention to adopt `tenant` claim to describe the issuer's tenant for a multi-tenant IdP.  The ID-JAG acts as a cross-domain Identity Assertion so it should assert an identity similar to an id token issued by the IdP for the resource app

[Resource, Audience, and Scope](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693#name-relationship-between-resour) are linked as you need all 3 to uniquely identify an authorization delegation for an AS and ensure there isn't a mix-up attack with an ambiguous scope name for example.  These have existing foundation in the security properties of the token request and I don't think we should be trying to overload.  These values should be consistent across OAuth specs and may be discovered with Protected Resource Metadata or Authorization Server metadata for example.

The ID-JAG audience (the one processing the ID-JAG) is the [Resource App's Authorization Server identifier ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-rfc7523bis-03#name-updates-to-rfc-7523) and must be unique within the IdP tenant as it functions as the cross-domain identifier to give the IdP context of the cross-domain request while resource+scope is relative to the Resource App's Authorization Server and may not be unique within the IdP tenant.  I think you may be identifying a gap here as that AS may be multi-tenant but the identifier isn't and when used a key there isn't a way to have multiple instances for different tenants.  This would be something like `aud_tenant` similar to `aud_sub` in https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-enterprise-extensions-1_0.html#name-aud_sub.  Its not clear how the IdP obtains this value and how its bound.

The ID-JAG presenter is a client that is registered in the Resource App's Authorization Server.  There is currently undefined behavior on how the IdP selects what client in the Resource App Authorization Server the ID-JAG should be used by and can act as the user.  This IdP can assert any client it wants and the Resource App Authorization Server needs to determine what it trusts.  We currently don't require client authentication is required for the ID-JAG token request to the Resource App Authorization Server (its vague).  Providing some security considerations and optionally some processing instructions was the goal of #45.   There is also an open issue to define how to bind the ID-JAG to a key so that the presenter must demonstrate proof of possession #28 .  If we require client authentication or DPOP for the ID-JAG than only a client that knows the secret/key/etc can use the the ID-JAG.  This should help with mix-up attacks/etc.

My reading of this issue is the following

- The Resource App Authorization Server identifier is multi-tenant (e.g doesn't have tenant in the identifier such `http://as.example.com`)
- The Resource App Authorization Server has a per-tenant client registration and the client identifier is unique across tenants
- The protected resource that the client wants to obtain cross-domain access to isn't tenant specific (e.g `https://rs.example.com`)

Not sure if the subject that the ID-JAG asserts resolves to an account in a specific Resource App tenant or not.  Would each environment (e.g development vs production) have a different subject identifier for the user?  What does the IdP put into an ID Token for SSO to these instances?

I think the issue of selecting the client for the ID-JAG might be similar to user as well if there is one to many relationship between the IdP the Resource App tenants and accounts.  An ID-JAG currently doesn't identify a Resource App tenant but rather this handled by processing the Resource App processing the `iss`, `sub`, `tenant` of the identity assertion and the `client_id`.

comments.author: dlozlla
comments.body:
Thanks for the context and the explanation, @mcguinness !

I think your reading of the issue is accurate. The Resource App AS is multi-tenant while the `audience`, `resource` and `client_id` - used by the Requesting App - are unique across tenants. To make things a bit more complex, the same IdP user `sub` can map to multiple of these tenants, but I think you’re spot on in saying that determining the tenant may follow the same procedures that are used to do the same for SSO flows. In those cases, we either:

1.  ask the end user <- this is not an option in this case
2. receive the id of the tenant in the login request, or 
3. infer it from sort of the “account” being used on the Resource App AS - we really call them connections and they represent a specific integration with a federated upstream IdP. Several of these accounts may map to the same IdP user but they define a local difference, let’s say a different local user, we can work with.

Focussing on option 3: for normal SSO, each of these “accounts”/connections map to a specific `client_id` on the IdP, that is used to start the login flow from the Resource App AS tenant. It is the `client_id` that would be used to sign in if the user clicks on that specific “Resource App instance” (e.g the datadog-dev app instance in our example) on the IdP SSO dashboard. This is precisely the piece of information I think we’re missing and we need to receive in the ID-JAG. Resource app isn't really an OIDC or OAuth term so I prefer to avoid using that term in claim names. issues.title: Discovering allowed Resource App (instances) for the logged in user
issues.author: dlozlla
issues.body:
As raised in issue https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/issues/51, a seamless user experience requires that Requesting Apps have a way to discover which applications, and their specific instances, a user is allowed to access. This would allow mirroring the experience of SSO dashboards, where users can simply select the app instance they want to use.

This raises several questions:
- Should the IdP expose an "Accessible Resources API" to list the available Resource Apps and their instances for an authenticated user?
- How should such an API structure its data to clearly differentiate between multiple instances of the same application?
- **Should this API be standardized?**

comments.author: meghnadubey
comments.body:
While the need for this API may be generic, the schema will be specific to the particular IdP implementation of IdAssertion Authz Grant setup and will be difficult to standardize. 
The API for any IdP will depend on how it is facilitating the setting up of secure "virtual connection" between requesting instances and resource instances, for the IT Admin. So this API is basically a form of get connections API that supports intuitive search for  a particular app, and most likely this API schema in some form will be part of any IdP implementation. 
We can definitely set up a recommendation, but I'm skeptical upon the practicality of standardizing it.

issues.title: Add Token Exchange support for refresh token instead of id token for ID-JAG
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
Since Refresh Tokens should not be returned when exchanging ID-JAG for an Access Token with the Resource Authorization Server, the Client will need to make an extra round-trip to the IDP Authorization Server to renew an ID Token using the IDP's Refresh Token so it can obtain a fresh ID-JAG with the new ID Token.   See https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-01.html#name-refresh-token

Adding support for `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:refresh_token` as the `subject_token` in the ID-JAG Token Exchange request would eliminate the round-trip needed to obtain the ID Token first as the IdP Authorization Server can dereference the refresh token to obtain the same claims that would be present in the ID Token.

We should also consider recommending that the IdP Authorization Server MAY return a `refresh_token` when exchanging a `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:saml2` token as the `subject_token` for an ID-JAG.  This would enable a Client that uses SAML for SSO to obtain a refresh token that they can use to renew ID-JAGs without having to switch to OIDC or redirect the user over the front channel.

I initially considered that flow but the  IdP would still need to issue a Refresh Token for the Client to obtain new ID Tokens after the SAML Assertion expires.   I suspect the need for a refresh token would be more common than just a single access token (SAML2->ID Token->ID-JAG->Access Token).  Since the goal is the ID-JAG and not the ID Token and there needs to be a way to obtain new ID-JAGs from the IdP, the optimized flow was to just add support for Refresh Token as the input vs RT->ID Token, ID-Token->ID-JAG, ID-JAG->Access Token.  It felt like the complexity still remains in the IdP and not the Client or the Resource AS which was our design goal and the IdP already understands its own refresh tokens.

Open to feedback here.

> Does this mean offline_access scope will be recommended when requesting id_token

Yes, if the client wants to obtain new Access Tokens when they expire for the Resource Server.

issues.title: Audience vs Resource Clarity
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body: We made the choice to require `audience` to be the Resource AS identifier and `resource` to be the protected resource for the Resource AS in this spec for interoperability.  While this approach seems allowed from how the Token Exchange spec is written, it isn't obvious to some readers who are familiar with Token Exchange.  We are effective profiling `audience` as the trust domain identifier vs defining a new param.  We don't need to change our decision but I think it may help to better state why we made this choice and provide some examples of multi-tenant resource authorization servers to help the reader understand how this profile is using audience and resource. Note that audience vs resource is a historically confusing problem across the specs.

issues.title: Add recommendations/considerations for user provisioning
issues.author: vsinghania-stytch
issues.body:
In the flow proposed by this draft, it is possible for a client to send a token exchange request concerning a user that the resource authorization server has never seen before, e.g. (using the terminology in 4.1) if I try to connect the chat app to the wiki app using my enterprise IdP without ever having created a chat app account.

What should happen in this scenario? I see a few options:
1. The chat app should take the ID-JAG token subject to the IdP and JIT provision a user based on the IdP's response. I think this would lead to a somewhat meaningless grant -- if I don't have a chat app account, what exactly would the wiki app gain from this anyway? Also, depending on the chat app's UX, this might spring a whole user onboarding flow on the user in the middle of the authz request.
2. The chat app should return a user not found error to the wiki app. I think this makes the most sense.
3. The IdP should not even issue an ID-JAG if it knows the user doesn't have a chat app account. This relies on the IdP always knowing whether the account exists, with high confidence, so I'm not sure it's a viable option.

In any case, I think it'd be helpful for the draft to address this scenario.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
This is currently an app & deployment-specific behavior.  

- A resource authorization server MAY choose to JIT provision an account using claims in the ID-JAG similar to JIT from ID Token or it MAY choose to reject the token request with an Oauth error response if an account is not successfully resolved.   
- Enterprises may use an external IGA system or workflow for account provisioning which the IdP Authorization Server may not have knowledge of.
- A provisioned account may not have a valid subscription/license or the correct entitlements for the scopes in the ID-JAG.

A client should not assume that obtaining the ID-JAG from the IdP is a guarantee that the ID-JAG is valid for the Resource AS and needs to handle OAuth error responses from the ID-JAG token request.  

Its not clear that a client needs a specific error code to handle the scenario where it Resource Authorization Server is unable to JIT provision an account for an unknown resource owner vs the currently defined generic `invalid_grant` error.

comments.author: vsinghania-stytch
comments.body: It seems reasonable to leave JIT provisioning as an optional feature. Curious if you think it'd be useful to include verbiage similar to your first point in the draft, e.g. under 4.4? I suspect a lot of resource AS implementations will wonder if JIT provisioning is allowed.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
There's a mention of this in the latest draft now: https://drafts.oauth.net/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant.html#section-3.1

> It is RECOMMENDED that the ID-JAG contain an email [[OpenID.Core](https://drafts.oauth.net/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant.html#OpenID.Core)] and/or aud_sub [[OpenID.Enterprise](https://drafts.oauth.net/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant.html#OpenID.Enterprise)] claim. The Resource Authorization Server MAY use these claims for account resolution or just-in-time (JIT) account creation, for example when the user has not yet SSO'd into the Resource Authorization Server. Additional Resource Authorization Server specific identity claims MAY be needed for account resolution or JIT account creation.

issues.title: Identifying the ID-JAG tenant in multi-tenant resource authorization servers
issues.author: vsinghania-stytch
issues.body:
When a resource authorization server (_not_ the enterprise IdP) is multi-tenanted, the AS needs to be able to uniquely identify the user _and_ the tenant that the ID-JAG is referring to. If the enterprise IdP doesn't use [pairwise identifiers](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#PairwiseAlg), it is not possible to identify the tenant using the required claims. If the IdP does use pairwise identifiers, the tenant can be identified _if_ the user + tenant combination has already been provisioned at the AS (or if SCIM is enabled).

We think this problem can be solved using the optional `tenant` claim in the draft. The resource AS can pre-register the value when the OIDC connection is configured, and the IdP can attach it to ID-JAGs.

A couple of questions about this:
1. Is this an intended/appropriate use of the `tenant` field?
2. The draft refers to the [OpenID.Enterprise definition of `tenant`](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-enterprise-extensions-1_0.html#section-2.2). This definition feels a bit confusing in the ID-JAG context -- why would the field ever have the value `organization`?
3. Is this worth calling out as a consideration?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: The `tenant` claim identifies the IdP tenant (issuer) and not the Resource Authorization Server tenant.  The intention of the ID-JAG is to mirror the same identity claims that the Resource Authorization Server obtains via an ID Token for uniquely identifying users via iss+tenant+sub.  This simplifies account resolution as the same logic can be applied for SSO and ID-JAG processing.  It doesn't address multi-tenant resource authorization servers that share the same authorization server identifier + client_id for a given IdP iss+tenant+sub.  This issue is discussed in  #51 .

comments.author: vsinghania-stytch
comments.body: Gotcha, that makes sense. I'll follow along + jump in on the linked issue. Closing this one – thanks!

issues.title: Proposal: Workload/Agent Identity SSO and Explicit Delegated “On-Behalf-Of” Access
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
# Proposal:  Workload /Agent Identity SSO and Explicit Delegated “On-Behalf-Of” Access

## Objective

Extend the **OAuth Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG)** specification so that:

1. The **IdP Authorization Server (AS-A)** can, **by policy**, determine how identity and delegation are represented when minting an ID-JAG for a **Resource Authorization Server (AS-B)**.
2. The **ID-JAG defines a common JWT assertion format used between authorization servers to convey identity and delegation context**, regardless of which identity or delegation model is used.

This proposal enables:

- **Workload/Agent Identity SSO** — a service or autonomous agent authenticating as itself across authorization domains  
- **Delegated “On-Behalf-Of” Access** — a client, workload, or AI agent acting using a user’s authority  
- A **uniform JWT-based assertion format** between Resource Authorization Server and IdP Authorization Server that works across all models  

The extension:

- **Preserves the existing OAuth user delegation model**
- Makes delegation **explicit when supported**
- Enables **workload identity** and future **actor chains**
- Allows **backward compatibility** for Resource AS that only understand traditional user delegation assertions
- Introduces **no new JWT claim registrations**
- Normatively depends on [**OAuth Entity Profiles**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mora-oauth-entity-profiles/)
- Reuses the **RFC 8693 `act` claim** for explicit delegation
- Supports [**IETF WIMSE Workload Identity Credentials**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds/) as an input actor credential format

## Identity & Delegation Models the IdP May Apply

The existing specification supports the widely deployed implicit delegation model of a client acting on behalf of a user. The `sub` claim of the ID-JAG always represents a user and the `client_id` is the application registered in the Resource Authorization Server that is acting on behalf of the user.

This extension does **not replace** that model but provides the following:

- Preserves the implicit model for compatibility
- Allows delegation to be made explicit using `act` claim
- Adds support for workloads or AI agents acting independently

When issuing an ID-JAG for a Resource Authorization Server, the IdP Authorization Server selects the delegation model and identity mapping based on what the client provided and IdP Authorization Server defined policy.

| Model | Meaning | ID-JAG Representation | Resource Authorization Server Compatibility |
|------|---------|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Client Acting as User (Existing OAuth Model)** | Client acts for user (implicit) | `sub = user` | Existing delegation model that is widely deployed today |
| **Explicit User Delegation** | Client/workload explicitly shown as actor | `sub = user`, `act = client/workload` | Requires actor-aware Resource Authorization Server |
| **Workload or Agent Acting as Itself (Workload SSO)** | No user involved | `sub = workload` or `sub = ai-agent` | Requires workload or AI-agent-aware Resource Authorization Server |
| **Compatibility Mapping** | Workload translated to legacy identity | Policy-mapped identity | For legacy Resource Authorization Server only |

## 1. ID-JAG as the Common JWT Assertion Between Authorization Servers

ID-JAG defines a **common JWT assertion format used between authorization servers to convey identity and delegation context**.

Regardless of identity model:

- Resource Authorization Server validates a **single JWT structure**
- Identity semantics (user, workload, AI-agent, delegation) are conveyed **within the same assertion**
- Resource Authorization Server relies on IdP Authorization Server policy for identity composition and delegation enforcement

This establishes a stable federation boundary while allowing identity semantics to evolve.

## 2. Normative Dependencies

The draft adds normative references to:

- [**OAuth Entity Profiles**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mora-oauth-entity-profiles/)
- [**IETF WIMSE Workload Identity Credentials**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-wimse-workload-creds/)

ID-JAG adds support for the following existing claims from Entity Profiles:

- `sub_profile`
- `client_profile`

IdP Authorization Server publishes additional Authorization Server metadata:

- `entity_profiles_supported`

No new claim registrations are introduced.

## 3. IdP Policy Determines ID-JAG Structure

During Token Exchange, IdP Authorization Server evaluates:

- Target audience (`aud` = Resource Authorization Server) to determine the trust relationship, token requirements, and delegation model
- Supplied credentials (user token, workload token, or both)
- Delegation grants and enterprise policy
- Resource Authorization Server capability profile

### Support for WIMSE Workload Credentials

When a workload presents an **actor credential** conforming to the WIMSE Workload Identity Credentials specification, the IdP Authorization Server:

- MAY accept the WIMSE credential as an `actor_token` in a Token Exchange request
- Validates the credential according to WIMSE processing rules and local trust policy
- Derives the workload identity used in the `act` claim or `sub` claim (for workload SSO)

This enables interoperable workload identity federation using a standardized workload credential format.

The IdP Authorization Server then selects the appropriate identity model and issues an ID-JAG that reflects the selected delegation model and context.

### A. Existing User Delegation (Implicit Model)

```
sub = user
sub_profile = user
(no act claim)
```

Maintains full backward compatibility.

### B. Explicit Delegation (Modern On-Behalf-Of)

```
sub = user
sub_profile = user
act.sub = client/workload
act.sub_profile includes "service" or "ai-agent" (if non-user)
```

Makes delegation visible and enforceable.

### C. Workload Identity SSO (Acting as Self)

```
sub = workload
sub_profile includes "service" or other non-user profile
```

Enables cross-domain workload SSO.

### D. Agent Identity SSO (Acting as Self)

```
sub = ai-agent
sub_profile includes "ai-agent"
```

Enables cross-domain AI agent SSO.

### E. Compatibility Mapping

IdP Authorization Server maps identities into a representation Resource Authorization Server understands when native workload, AI-agent, or actor support is absent.

Mapping is **policy-controlled**, not client-controlled.

## 4. Resource AS Processing Rules

Resource Authorization Server processes the **same ID-JAG assertion format** in all cases.

| Condition | Resource Authorization Server Behavior |
|----------|-----------------------------------------|
| `act` present | Perform dual-principal authorization |
| No `act`, `sub_profile=user` | Standard user authorization |
| No `act`, `sub_profile=service` | Workload acting as self |
| No `act`, `sub_profile=ai-agent` | AI agent acting as self |
| Compatibility mapping | Process as normal legacy identity |

## 5. Access Token Issuance

Resource Authorization Server issues tokens preserving the identity model expressed in the ID-JAG.

Permissions must be the **intersection** of:

- User rights (if present)
- Workload/Agent rights
- Delegation grants
- Requested scope/resource
- Requested Authorization Details

## 6. Sender-Constraining Guidance

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|----------|----------------|
| Existing OAuth user model | Existing guidance applies |
| Explicit delegation (`act`) | SHOULD use sender-constrained tokens |
| Workload acting as self | SHOULD use sender-constrained tokens |
| Compatibility mapping | SHOULD use sender-constraining if workload-originated |

## 7. Metadata and Discovery

No new ID-JAG metadata is defined.

Authorization Servers supporting this extension **SHOULD** publish:

```
entity_profiles_supported
```

IdP Authorization Server maintains internal policy describing Resource Authorization Server capability levels.

## 8. IANA Impact

None.

- No new JWT claim registrations
- No new registries
- Reuses Entity Profiles and RFC 8693 `act`

## Final Outcome

| Goal | How It Is Achieved |
|------|--------------------|
| Preserve existing OAuth delegation | Keep implicit user model unchanged |
| Support workload or AI Agent identity SSO | `sub_profile` indicates service or ai-agent |
| Support delegated on-behalf-of access | `sub` = user + `act` = workload |
| Provide common AS-to-AS assertion | ID-JAG JWT assertion format |
| Support legacy systems | IdP compatibility mapping |
| Enable future actor chains | Policy-driven evolution |
| Keep single client interface | IdP decides representation per AS |
| Avoid new claims | Reuse Entity Profiles + `act` |

This extension establishes ID-JAG as a **common JWT assertion format between authorization servers**, enabling both **workload identity SSO** and **delegated user access** while remaining fully backward compatible.

comments.author: kennethsinder
comments.body:
Implementer feedback in support of the explicit on-behalf-of / actor direction here, from building a multi-agent runtime that consumes MCP servers through enterprise-managed authorization (which uses ID-JAG).

**The concrete case where today's single-subject shape loses information:** a user delegates to an orchestrator agent, which delegates a subtask to a specialized sub-agent, which reaches an MCP server through enterprise-managed auth. The token that arrives at the resource carries one delegated subject; the intermediate hops are gone. Everything downstream that wants to answer "which human caused this write, through which chain of software actors?" has to reconstruct it by joining logs across every hop, and each hop represents identity differently. An explicit `act` chain in the assertion, as proposed here, is what removes that reconstruction.

Two properties from running this shape in production that I'd advocate keeping as the draft firms up:

1. **Nested actors stay audit-only.** Authorization decisions come from the top-level token claims and the current actor; the nested chain is attribution history and must not be a way to acquire access. Keeping that line bright is what makes carrying the chain safe. Otherwise every entry in the chain becomes an attack surface.
2. **Per-hop scope visibility is worth the bytes.** Recording the scopes each actor held at its hop makes authority attenuation auditable (you can see the chain narrowing). We've found this is the difference between an audit record that answers questions and one that raises them.

Happy to provide more implementation detail if useful to the authors.

*Disclosure: drafted with AI assistance and reviewed before posting.*

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
@kennethsinder, have you taken a look at https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile/? 

ID-JAG processing rules were relaxed to allow `actor_token` to be passed on the token exchange request to enable profiles like the Actor Profile to be layered ontop.  We didn't want to push normative requirements for per-hop visibility and provenance processing into the core ID-JAG spec.

comments.author: kennethsinder
comments.body:
@mcguinness Thanks, and apologies for the slow reply. I've read both the Actor Profile draft and ID-JAG-04, and they do answer most of what I raised.

Some thoughts:

- **The nested-`act` representation is what I was missing, and it's stronger than what I asked for.** "Delegation chains MUST be represented by nesting `act` objects", combined with the requirement that an AS "MUST NOT silently drop an inbound `act` claim; if it cannot preserve or extend the chain, it MUST reject the request", closes the failure mode I actually care about. Silent truncation is worse than rejection for anyone reconstructing a chain after the fact, because the resulting token still looks well-formed and simply attributes the work to the wrong principal. Fail-closed is the right default here.

- **The (`act.iss`, `act.sub`) pair as the canonical identifier is a migration hazard worth making explicit.** Implementations predating the profile are likely to key an actor on `sub` alone, which collides across issuers. It may be worth an explicit note in security considerations that comparing `act.sub` without `act.iss` is unsafe; could be the kind of thing that works silently in a single-IdP deployment and breaks on the first cross-domain hop.

**Two things the profile deliberately leaves open, which is where my remaining questions sit.** The draft states it "does not standardize the policies by which systems determine whether a given actor is permitted to act for a subject", and that members carried inside an `act` object "do not have standardized proof-of-possession semantics".

Those are the two I keep landing on from the implementation side, and there's an independent convergence worth highlighting: a parallel discussion in the A2A community ([a2aproject/A2A#2028](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/2028)) reached the same split from a different direction; its framing seems useful:

1. **Per-hop scope narrowing is a well-formedness check and not proof of authority.** If each hop carries its scopes and each hop's scopes must be a subset of its predecessor's, a verifier can detect a downstream actor claiming authority its upstream never held, from the payload alone, with no cross-hop log join. But because the chain is caller-supplied, a fabricated chain can narrow perfectly at every step. Narrowing tells you the chain does not self-contradict; it says nothing about whether any hop was granted what it claims.
2. **Proof of grant needs a per-hop reference that a verifier resolves without trusting the payload.** And absence of such a reference should not be readable as evidence that nothing was granted, only that no reconciliation aid was provided.

My question: is the intent that both stay permanently deployment-specific, or is there room for a companion profile that pins the well-formedness half — the subset relation and its failure mode — while leaving grant policy entirely local? The first looks standardizable without constraining anyone's authorization policy, since it's a consistency property over the chain rather than a rule about who may act for whom.

Happy to write that up as a concrete proposal if useful, or to leave it be if you would rather keep the profile focused.

---

issues.title: Potential Usecase: Whitelabeling of SaaS Services
issues.author: max-stytch
issues.body:
I have a variation of the usecases described in sections `A.2` and `A.3` that may be interesting to talk through. I think authentication for whitelabled SaaS components could be a strong application of XAA. There are other less standardized approaches for this problem today.

----

## Intro

SaaS platforms often purchase and re-expose whitelabeled capabilities from other SaaS platforms. For example,
functionality like comments sections, chat widgets, support bots, or email notifications can often be sold as standalone features and embedded into customer-facing applications. 

This functionality may consist of UI elements, APIs, or the combination of both to create full-stack widgets. When an end user interacts with one of these widgets,it is advantageous to use OAuth access tokens to authorize the interaction so the widget understand the user identity. For example, a comments section widget might allow users to edit their own comment, but not the comments of other users. A feedback widget might want to aggregate feedback by user, or might want to only accept feedback from authenticated users.

Today, there are a few common approaches for whitelabeled authentication usecases:

- Completely unauthenticated widgets like Google Maps use [public API Keys](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/demo-key). These public keys are highly abusable. Attackers that scrape the key can use it to exhaust API quotas and drive up usage bills. No calls within the Google Maps system can be tied back to an end user identity.

- Svix does away with OAuth and access tokens entirely, and has the website backend generate a [pre-signed URL](https://docs.svix.com/app-portal#giving-your-users-access) for the frontend to use. This method is more secure than a completely public API, but still loses the user identity context. 

- The whitelabel resource server could be preconfigured to accept tokens issued by the CIAM IDP directly - like how Supabase can accept access tokens [issued by Auth0](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/third-party/auth0). This approach typically only works with JWT access tokens that adhere to a specific & interoperable format. Access tokens in a bespoke or nonstandard format are much more difficult to validate. This approach also pushes a lot of complexity on the resource server - which may accept access tokens from hundreds or thousands of ASs.

I believe XAA can be used here instead to create a standardized approach.

----

## Applying XAA

Let's take the `wiki.example` case and assume that the wiki app developers want to whitelabel a feedback widget to 
collect feedback from authenticated users on each page. 

This flow differs from other examples already documented in the following ways:
- The IDP Authorization Server is the CIAM AS, operated by the application developer
- The application developer is the persona setting policy considerations
- The client is a first-party application to the IDP AS
- The client is integrated with both the IDP AS and the Resource Server AS - no dynamic discovery of AS information is needed during the flow.

We have the following entities in the system:

```
  +======================+================================+================================================+
  | Role                 | App URL                        | Description                                    |
  +======================+================================+================================================+
  | Client               | https://wiki.example           | Wiki app that embeds content from one or more  |
  |                      |                                | resource servers                               |
  +----------------------+--------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
  | Identity Provider    | https://auth.wiki.example      | CIAM Identity Provider for the wiki app        |
  | Authorization Server |                                |                                                |
  +----------------------+--------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
  | Resource             | https://auth.feedback.example  | Authorization Server for a customer feedback   |
  | Authorization Server |                                | service                                        |
  +----------------------+--------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
  | Resource Server      | https://api.feedback.example   | Public API for the customer feedback service   |
  +----------------------+--------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
```

## Preconditions
- The First Party App has a registered OAuth 2.0 Client (`com.example.wiki`) with the CIAM IdP (`auth.wiki.example`)
- The First Party App has a registered OAuth 2.0 Client (`18723649238176`) with the Whitelabel AS (`auth.feedback.example`)
- Application Developer has established a trust relationship between their CIAM IdP and the First Party App for SSO
- Application Developer has established a trust relationship between their CIAM IdP and the Whitelabel AS for SSO and Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant
- Application Developer has granted the First Party App permission to act on behalf of users within the Whitelabel API with a specific set of scopes

## Example Sequence

### First Party App establishes a User Identity with CIAM IdP

#### IdP Authorization Request (with PKCE)
First Party App generates a PKCE code_verifier and a code_challenge (usually a SHA256 hash of the verifier, base64url-encoded) and redirects the end-user to the CIAM IdP with an authorization request
```
GET /authorize?
  response_type=code
  &client_id=com.example.wiki
  &redirect_uri=https://wiki.example/oauth2/callback
  &scope=openid+profile+email
  &state=xyzABC123
  &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
  &code_challenge_method=S256
Host: auth.wiki.example
```
No explicit user authorization step is required as the application is considered first party. 
The CIAM IdP authenticates the end-user and redirects back to the First Party App's registered client redirect URI with an authorization code:

    https://wiki.example/oauth2/callback?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA&state=xyzABC123

First Party App exchanges the code and PKCE code_verifier to obtain an ID Token and Access Token for the IdP's UserInfo endpoint

```
POST /oauth2/token
Host: auth.wiki.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
&redirect_uri=https://wiki.example/oauth2/callback
&client_id=com.example.wiki
&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
"id_token": "eyJraWQiOiJzMTZ0cVNtODhwREo4VGZCXzdrSEtQ...",
"token_type": "Bearer",
"access_token": "7SliwCQP1brGdjBtsaMnXo",
"scope": "openid profile email"
}
```
First Party App validates the ID Token using the published JWKS for the IdP
```
{
"iss": "https://auth.wiki.example/",
"sub": "1997e829-2029-41d4-a716-446655440000",
"aud": "com.example.wiki",
"exp": 1984444800,
"iat": 1684441200,
"auth_time": 1684440000,
"name": "John Connor",
"email": "john.connor@cyberdyne.example",
"email_verified": true
}
```

###  First Party App calls Whitelabeled API

As the First Party App is integrated directly with the Whitelabeled API, no AS discovery step is necessary.
The App can proceed directly to requesting an ID-JAG for token exchange.

#### First Party App obtains an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant for Whitelabeled API from the CIAM IdP
First Party App makes an ID-JAG token exchange request to the CIAM IdP. It presents the ID Token obtained in the previous step, along with the scopes and resource identifier for the whitelabel API (both preconfigured by the developer)
```
POST /oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.wiki.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&audience=https://auth.feedback.example/
&resource=https://api.feedback.example/
&scope=feedback.submit
&subject_token=eyJraWQiOiJzMTZ0cVNtODhwREo4VGZCXzdrSEtQ...
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
&client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIyIn0...
```
If access is granted, the CIAM IDP creates a signed Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant and returns it in the token exchange response.
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-store
Pragma: no-cache

{
"issued_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag",
"access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsI...",
"token_type": "N_A",
"scope": "feedback.submit",
"expires_in": 300
}
```
Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant claims:
```
{
"alg": "ES256",
"typ": "oauth-id-jag+jwt"
}
.
{
"jti": "9e43f81b64a33f20116179",
"iss": "https://auth.wiki.example",
"sub": "1llb-b4c0-0000-8000-t800b4ck0000",
"aud": "https://auth.feedback.example",
"resource": "https://api.feedback.example/",
"client_id": "18723649238176",
"exp": 1984445160,
"iat": 1984445100,
"scope": "feedback.submit"
}
.
signature
```
#### First Party App obtains an Access Token for Whitelabel API
First Party App makes a token request to the previously registered whitelabel API's Authorization Server token endpoint using the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant obtained from the CIAM IDP as a JWT Assertion.

The First Party App authenticates with its client credentials that were registered with the Whitelabel API's Authorization Server

```
POST /oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.feedback.example
Authorization: Basic yZS1yYW5kb20tc2VjcmV0v3JOkF0XG5Qx2

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
assertion=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsI...
```
Whitelabel API's Authorization Server validates the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant using the published JWKS for the trusted CIAM IDP
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json;charset=UTF-8
Cache-Control: no-store
Pragma: no-cache

{
"token_type": "Bearer",
"access_token": "2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA",
"expires_in": 86400,
"scope": "feedback.submit"
}
```
#### First Party App makes an authorized Whitelabel API request
First Party App invokes a Whitelabel API provided by the Resource Server with a valid access token
```
POST /feedback/submit
Host: api.feedback.example
Authorization: Bearer 2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA"
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
...
}
```

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body:
My colleague @vsinghania-stytch pointed out another variant of this flow that would not be strictly compliant with XAA but would use the same well-defined XAA functionality between trust domains. What happens if a developer moves the resource server client responsibilities from the first-party app to the IdP AS? A developer could make the IdP AS responsible for generating the ID-JAG and exchanging it with the Resource Server AS, and then have the IdP AS return the granted access token directly to the client.

After a bit of digging, I realized this is essentially `B.2.  Authorization server acting as client` from `I-D.ietf-oauth-identity-chaining`. Are those use cases identified in section B (AS as Client and RS as Client) within the scope of XAA?

For a practical application, see existing Token Vault functionality ([ex1](https://auth0.com/docs/secure/call-apis-on-users-behalf/token-vault), [ex2](https://auth0.com/docs/secure/call-apis-on-users-behalf/token-vault)) where the IdP AS stores access and refresh tokens from other trust domains, and dispenses those access and refresh tokens to clients internally. In Token Vaults today, these access and refresh tokens come from `auth_code` flows and require user involvement. With XAA, the IdP AS could mint access tokens for external resources on demand instead. 

Preconditions:
- The First Party App has a registered OAuth 2.0 Client with the CIAM IdP 
- The CIAM IdP has a registered OAuth Client with the Whitelabel AS 
- Application Developer has established a trust relationship between their CIAM IdP and the First Party App for SSO
- Application Developer has established a trust relationship between their CIAM IdP and the Whitelabel AS for SSO and Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant


Steps:
1. First-Party App completes an `auth_code` flow and receives an ID Token and/or Access Token.
1. First-Party App initiates a token exchange, requesting an access token scoped to the Resource Server with some set of Resource Server specific scopes
1. The IdP AS mints an ID-JAG internally and sends the ID-JAG to the Resource Server AS as a JWT Assertion
1. The Resource Server AS validates the ID-JAG and issues an access token scoped to the Resource Server
1. The IDP AS returns the access token to the First-Party App
1. The First-Party App uses this access token to access the Resource Server

Reasons why a developer might pursue this model:
1. Simplifies development of First-Party App, which no longer needs to integrate with the Resource Server AS, and reduces # of API calls from 2 to 1
1. Many First-Party Apps can reuse a single access token for the Resource Server
1. Makes it possible for the IdP AS to mint & cache access tokens ahead of time, reducing overall system latency

Reasons why a developer might not pursue this model:
1. Resource Server AS loses insight into which client is actually being granted an access token
1. Incompatible with DPoP
1. Step (2) - the token exchange between the first-party app and the AS - is not tightly standardized

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
> What happens if a developer moves the resource server client responsibilities from the first-party app to the IdP AS?

The IdP acting as the Client would need client credentials to act as the client in the ID-JAG. This binds that the ID-JAG to the client registered with the Resource AS so that the ID-JAG can't impersonate any client. 

See  https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-02#name-cross-domain-client-id-hand

> The Client still needs to authenticate using its registered credential with the Resource Authorization Server when presenting the ID-JAG for the mapped client_id. Requiring a confidential client helps to prevent the IdP Authorization Server from delegating access to any of the valid clients for the Resource Authorization Server.

In your example, what client is the ID-JAG bound to?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: @max-stytch can you review #78

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body:
> In your example, what client is the ID-JAG bound to? The ID-JAG is bound to the IdP. The IdP acts as a Client registered in the Resource Server AS. In the example, the IdP mints the ID-JAG and immediately exchanges the ID-JAG for an access token, using its client credentials. Once the IdP receives an access token, the IdP can then choose to distribute that access token internally within its trust domain, following logic not defined by XAA. This means the access token can ultimately be used by software systems that are not known to the Resource Server AS (who only sees the Client ID of the IdP). Assume there are two clients: - `first_party_app` registered at the IdP - `acme_co_client` registered at the Resource Server AS - The IdP is configured with the `acme_co_client` credentials - The IdP returns the access token to the `first_party_app` afterwards ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as First-Party App participant IdP as IdP AS participant RAS as Resource Server AS participant RS as Resource Server App->>IdP: non-XAA Token Exchange Request
(requesting access token for Resource Server) IdP->>IdP: Mints ID-JAG internally IdP->>RAS: Present JWT Assertion as acme_co_client Note over RAS: Validates ID-JAG RAS-->>IdP: Access Token IdP-->>App: Access Token App->>RS: API Request with Access Token RS-->>App: Response ``` Would this "remixing" of the XAA flow in a way the Resource Server AS is unable to detect or prevent - be categorized as a valid use of XAA? or an invalid use that should be addressed?
