issues.title: Adding Optional `actor_token` to ID-JAG for Explicit Actor Modeling
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
# Adding Optional `actor_token` to ID-JAG for Explicit Actor Modeling

## Summary

The OAuth Identity Assertion Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) deliberately enforces **client continuity**:

- the `subject_token` was issued to a specific OAuth client
- that same client (`client_id`) MUST present the `subject_token` when requesting the ID-JAG

This is a strong and desirable property. It prevents cross-client substitution and ensures that the OAuth client that obtained the upstream subject credential is the one continuing the flow.

However, client continuity and actor identity are not the same thing.

Client continuity answers:

> Which OAuth client continued the flow?

Many delegated systems also need to answer:

> Which actor actually exercised the subject’s authorization?

In simple deployments, those two identities may coincide. In more complex deployments, they often do not.

This issue proposes adding **optional support for an `actor_token`** so that deployments that need explicit actor fidelity can represent it directly, while preserving ID-JAG’s current client-continuity guarantees.

## Current Model: Client Continuity as Implicit Actor

ID-JAG today enforces:

```text
subject_token -> issued to client A
ID-JAG request -> must be made by client A
```

This guarantees:

> the same OAuth client that received the subject token is the one continuing the authorization flow

That is an important security property because it:
- prevents one client from replaying another client’s subject credential
- preserves the RP/client binding of the original identity assertion
- provides a simple and robust model for traditional RP-to-API scenarios

In effect, the current design treats the authenticated client as the implicit actor.

## The Gap: Client Continuity Is Not Actor Fidelity

The current model proves continuity of the OAuth client. It does not necessarily prove fidelity of the acting principal.

That distinction matters because `client_id` identifies an OAuth client registration, not necessarily the execution principal that is acting on behalf of the subject at runtime.

In modern systems, a single client may front:
- multiple services
- multiple workloads
- multiple agent instances
- multiple execution environments
- both human-initiated and automated execution paths

In those architectures, the current model guarantees:

> client A continued the flow

but it does not guarantee:

> actor X, rather than actor Y, actually exercised the subject’s authorization

### Where the Current Model Falls Short

### 1. Multiple Actors Behind a Single Client

A single `client_id` may represent multiple distinct acting entities.

Example:

```text
client_id = "frontend-app"

frontend-app
  -> orchestration layer
     -> agent A executes task
     -> agent B executes task
```

Both requests:
- use the same `client_id`
- satisfy the current ID-JAG continuity rules

But:
- actor A and actor B are not the same principal
- they may differ in trust level, permissions, or execution context
- downstream services cannot distinguish them if only client identity is preserved

### 2. Delegation Within the Same Client Boundary

A user may initiate a flow through an RP, and an automated agent may later continue it under the same client registration.

From the current ID-JAG model, nothing has changed:
- same `client_id`
- same flow continuity

But operationally:
- the acting entity has changed
- the security, audit, and authorization semantics have changed
- downstream systems may need to know that the request is now being executed by an agent rather than by the original front-end context

#### 3. Loss of Actor Context for Downstream Consumers

Without an explicit actor input, downstream components often see only:
- the issued token
- the client identity carried or inferred
- deployment-specific local context

They do not reliably learn:
- which execution principal acted
- whether a distinct delegated actor was involved
- how to represent that actor across trust boundaries

As a result, actor semantics become deployment-local rather than portable.

### 4. Overloading `client_id`

Using `client_id` as a stand-in for the actor conflates distinct concepts:

- OAuth client identity
- runtime actor identity
- delegated execution identity

That overloading works only when those identities happen to collapse to the same principal. When they diverge, the protocol has no explicit way to express the difference.

## Why This Matters

This is not only an observability issue. It affects:

- **authorization correctness**: policies may need to distinguish subject, client, and actor
- **audit fidelity**: logs should identify the actual delegated actor, not only the client registration
- **interoperability**: actor semantics cannot be carried cleanly across issuers if they are only inferred from local client context
- **security analysis**: confused-deputy and delegation review are harder when actor identity is implicit

See https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile.html for more discussion on Actor Chaining and Implicit Delegation

## Proposal: Optional `actor_token`

Define an optional request parameter:

```text
actor_token
```

The `actor_token` would:
- represent the entity acting on behalf of the subject
- be validated by the Authorization Server
- allow the AS to embed explicit actor information in the resulting JWT, for example via `act` per https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile.html

This would not replace the current client-continuity requirement. Rather:

- client continuity would continue to prove that the same OAuth client is continuing the flow
- `actor_token` would optionally provide explicit evidence of which actor is exercising the subject’s authorization

## Why Optional Support Is the Right Shape

This should be optional because:

- existing ID-JAG deployments should continue to work unchanged
- many traditional RP-based flows do not need additional actor modeling
- explicit actor representation is most valuable in multi-actor, multi-hop, or cross-domain delegated systems

Optional `actor_token` support would therefore:
- preserve today’s security model
- avoid imposing new complexity on simple deployments
- enable explicit actor semantics where they are actually needed

## Benefits of Optional `actor_token`

Optional `actor_token` support would:

- preserve the current same-client continuity guarantee
- add first-class actor identity when client continuity is not sufficient
- reduce reliance on deployment-specific inference from `client_id`
- enable downstream tokens to carry explicit actor semantics
- improve audit and authorization fidelity in multi-actor systems
- better support delegated and cross-domain architectures

## Key Question

Client continuity answers which OAuth client continued the flow.

Should ID-JAG also support an optional, explicit mechanism for identifying which actor exercised the subject’s authorization when those are not the same principal?

issues.title: Interoperability gap: JIT provisioning and identity claim negotiation
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
# Problem

Section 2.1 of the draft currently says:

> It is RECOMMENDED that the ID-JAG contain an `email` and/or `aud_sub` claim. The Resource Authorization Server MAY use these claims for account resolution or just-in-time (JIT) account creation... Additional Resource Authorization Server specific identity claims MAY be needed for account resolution or JIT account creation.

This language acknowledges the JIT problem but does not solve it. There is no interoperable mechanism for a Resource Authorization Server (RAS) to signal which identity claims it requires, or for a Client to convey that signal back to the IdP so it can include them in the ID-JAG. The result requires out-of-band coordination between every IdP/RAS pair, which undermines the composability goal of the spec.

## Specific failure modes

1. **What claims does the IdP put in the ID-JAG?** The spec provides a fixed optional set (`email`, `aud_sub`) but gives no mechanism for the RAS to express its requirements. IdPs must either over-include claims (privacy risk) or guess conservatively and leave JIT broken.

2. **What claims does the RAS need to JIT?** RAS-specific claims (department, cost center, license tier, custom identifiers) may not be OIDC standard claims. Even for OIDC-defined claims, different RASes need different subsets. There is no way to express this per-RAS, per-deployment requirement today.

3. **How does the IdP know to issue the right claims?** The IdP has no standardized signal from the Client about what the target RAS needs. The Client knows the RAS endpoint (from discovery) but cannot ask the IdP to tailor the ID-JAG for that RAS's JIT requirements.

4. **The UserInfo dead end.** When the RAS receives the ID-JAG it has no Access Token and cannot reach back to the IdP's UserInfo endpoint or any other IdP-hosted endpoint to fetch additional claims. The ID-JAG exchange must succeed or fail on the claims already present in the token. This is not a fixable limitation; it is a structural constraint of the grant flow.

# Proposed Solution

Standardize exactly three things.

## 1. Error code: `insufficient_identity_claims`

If the RAS determines that the identity assertion is cryptographically valid and the grant type is accepted, but the token does not contain sufficient identity claims to perform account resolution or JIT account creation, it SHOULD return an error response per RFC 6749 Section 5.2:

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": "insufficient_identity_claims",
  "error_description": "The identity assertion is missing required claims for account resolution."
}
```

The name follows the `insufficient_*` pattern established by RFC 9470 (`insufficient_user_authentication`). It signals "valid but not enough", distinguishing this condition from `invalid_grant`, which would indicate the token itself is rejected. 

## 2. Error response parameter: `required_claims`

The error response SHOULD include a `required_claims` parameter: a space-separated list of the claim names the RAS requires, following the same format as `scope` (RFC 6749 Section 3.3):

```json
{
  "error": "insufficient_identity_claims",
  "error_description": "The identity assertion is missing required claims for account resolution.",
  "required_claims": "email department employee_number"
}
```

Space-separated is the right format here. Claim names are JSON member names and cannot contain spaces, so the delimiter is unambiguous. This is consistent with `scope` and avoids the framework-parsing ambiguity of a JSON array in a form-encoded body (cf. RFC 9396 `authorization_details`, which uses JSON because its values are structured objects; claim names are flat tokens and do not warrant that complexity).

`required_claims` is intentionally defined as a flat list of names. Value constraints, type hints, and schema references are deferred pending real deployment experience.

## 3. Token Exchange request extension parameter: `required_claims`

A Client receiving an `insufficient_identity_claims` error MAY retry the Token Exchange request to the IdP Authorization Server, including the `required_claims` parameter with the value carried directly from the RAS error response:

```
POST /oauth2/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&subject_token=<id_token>
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&audience=https://api.example.com/
&required_claims=email+department+employee_number
```

The symmetric naming (`required_claims` in both the error response and the Token Exchange request) means the Client can pass the value through without transformation. "Required" reflects the RAS's perspective, which is authoritative: these claims are required for the flow to succeed. It does not obligate the IdP to provide all of them; the IdP SHOULD include the requested claims subject to its own policy (consent, availability, privacy controls), and MAY decline to include specific claims.

## End-to-end flow

```
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange → ID-JAG (minimal claims)
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with ID-JAG
RAS → Client:    400 insufficient_identity_claims
                     required_claims=email department employee_number
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange + required_claims=email department employee_number
IdP → Client:    ID-JAG with additional claims included
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with enriched ID-JAG
RAS → Client:    200 OK, access_token
```

# Editorial: relax `email` and `aud_sub` to plain OPTIONAL

With `required_claims` providing the negotiation mechanism, the RECOMMENDED status of `email` and `aud_sub` in Section 2.1 should be downgraded to OPTIONAL. These claims become examples of what a RAS might request rather than a standing recommendation that every IdP include them. The existing guidance language should be replaced with a pointer to the `required_claims` mechanism as the interoperable way to express and negotiate claim requirements, and an example end-to-end flow demonstrating the retry pattern.

# Advanced use case: RAS Token Exchange to IdP

For deployments where the identity data needed cannot reasonably be pre-embedded in a signed token (because it is large, sensitive, or needs to be fresher than the ID-JAG allows), the RAS MAY perform its own Token Exchange: presenting the received ID-JAG as the subject token to the IdP's token endpoint and requesting an Access Token scoped to the IdP's identity APIs.

This covers the UserInfo-equivalent pattern without burdening the Client as intermediary, and without embedding what is effectively a profile API response inside the ID-JAG. It should be acknowledged in the spec as a valid deployment pattern with the IdP-side API contract left to a future profile. This keeps the core ID-JAG spec clean and avoids scope creep.

# Optional / future: claim requirements discovery at the RAS

To allow IdPs to import a RAS's claim requirements at onboarding time rather than waiting for a runtime error, the RAS could advertise the claims it needs for JIT provisioning via its Authorization Server metadata (RFC 8414), using a new metadata parameter scoped to this profile (to avoid collision with base OAuth or other profiles).

This is an optimization for IdP onboarding UX, not a correctness requirement. The runtime `insufficient_identity_claims` negotiation works without it. Worth raising for debate; not a blocker for the core proposal.

---

# Questions for the group

1. **Error name:** `insufficient_identity_claims` (cause, RFC 9470 pattern)  or alternative?
2. **IdP acknowledgment:** Should the IdP be required to indicate in the ID-JAG which claims from `required_claims` it was able to include, or is the Client expected to inspect the resulting token before retrying at the RAS?
3. **RAS-to-IdP Token Exchange:** Should the advanced pattern be noted in Security Considerations? The RAS acting as an OAuth client to the IdP has trust and SSRF implications worth calling out even if the pattern itself is out of scope.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
Interesting idea...

One concern that pops out immediately is the privacy leakage of the information to the client.

Normally the provisioning would happen server-to-server, and the user's data would be sent over TLS directly between the IdP and authorization server. This makes the client the transport mechanism of the data, which it could read from the unencrypted ID-JAG. 

Unfortunately the only ways to avoid this are significantly more complex (encrypted ID-JAG, encrypted claims in the ID-JAG, secondary provisioning protocol like OP Commands/SCIM).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Proposal addresses that in a **limited** way

- IdP determines if it wants to release the claims (meets policy/etc) 
- Escape hatch with RAS Token Exchange to IdP

In practice many deployments use standard OIDC claims where the values are the same profile used across apps.  Its the same data it already has access to via OIDC for example.   Yes there are pair-wise identifiers this could leak as well as other claims but you correctly identified the solution (encrypted ID-JAG).  

I have personally seen enough deployments to convince me that standard OIDC claims meet the need for JIT for many apps that this is valuable enough to have without adding encryption.  IdPs can choose to reject the claims so there is safe exit.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
Ok good point. If the OIDC claims are enough for JIT provisioning then this isn't any worse. It would be worth calling out explicitly that this is only for OIDC claims. Or if we don't want to actually require that, then at the very least a big security considerations section talking about the risk of including non-OIDC claims.

I was getting thrown off from the language about non-OIDC claims:

> RAS-specific claims (department, cost center, license tier, custom identifiers) may not be OIDC standard claims

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
Actually it's less important that they are OIDC-defined claims, and more important that the IdP only includes claims in the ID-JAG that it would have included in an ID Token.

The risk is then that the claims might have been pairwise and only the AS (domain B) would have gotten the claims for domain B, but now the client in domain A is getting the claims that will be provided to domain B. 

But to your point, if the limited claims that are OIDC defined are sufficient for most JIT use cases, it might be fine to just explain this in the security considerations.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
> Actually it's less important that they are OIDC-defined claims, and more important that the IdP only includes claims in the ID-JAG that it would have included in an ID Token.

Correct.  There are claims that sometimes may only be available over UserInfo (e.g large group graphs) that this wouldn't support.  This would require "RAS Token Exchange to IdP" so the RAS can obtain its own access token.   Custom RP claims can be used over ID Token

> The risk is then that the claims might have been pairwise and only the AS (domain B) would have gotten the claims for domain B, but now the client in domain A is getting the claims that will be provided to domain B.

Correct, this would need to be documented and would be decision for the IdP to make.  There may be apps an IdP operator is OK releasing this to. 

We can add ID-JAG encryption if folks think its worth it.  I think its easier to just implement "RAS Token Exchange to IdP" for those scenarios but biased.  Either way the privacy risks need to be documented.   Where I was hoping for more consensus is whether the base proposal has enough interoperability value to be useful knowing the risks.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body:
User creation is the main use case for JIT provisioning, but we should also consider user updates.

SSO logins are commonly used to synchronize user data. SCIM _is much better_ for this, but SCIM support is far less common than SSO support.

Consider the following:

1. A user is initially JIT created in the RAS by an ID-JAG flow. The user has an email of `email1@example.com`.

2. At some point in the future, the user's email changes from `email1@example.com` to `email2@example.com`. 
    * With a regular OIDC SSO flow, the RAS would be notified of the new email on the user's next OIDC login. 

What can the AS do?

### Option 1: Always Challenge
The RAS can _always_ issue an `insufficient_identity_claims` response, even when the user already exists. This forces the client to fetch a token with the latest section of claims, and guarantees that the RAS always gets the latest user information. This comes at the cost of added latency (2x more round trips!) 
```
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange → ID-JAG (minimal claims)
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with ID-JAG
RAS → Client:    400 insufficient_identity_claims
                     required_claims=email
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange + required_claims=email
IdP → Client:    ID-JAG with additional claims included
                     "email":"email2@example.com"
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with enriched ID-JAG
                     RAS updates user object
RAS → Client:    200 OK, access_token
```

### Option 2: Never Challenge
An RAS implementation could choose to not challenge at all, resulting in it operating on stale user data.

```
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange → ID-JAG (minimal claims)
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with ID-JAG
                     RAS references stale user object
RAS → Client:    200 OK, access_token
```

------

Both the `RAS Token Exchange to IdP` and `Claim Requirements Discovery at the RAS` approaches avoid this problem. 

In the `RAS Token Exchange to IdP` approach, the RAS receives the exact same ID token it would have received had it done a regular OIDC flow. Information parity is assured.

In the `Claim Requirements Discovery at the RAS` approach, the RAS can broadcast the scopes it requires and the IdP can create an appropriate ID-JAG, eliminating the round-trip.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Agree that if we adopt this proposal, it should have text that describes both create and update.  I also agree that `RAS Token Exchange to IdP` solves a lot of the edge cases. 

We first need to get consensus on

1. Should this spec make normative changes now to address JIT?
2. What is the preferred high level solution (this proposal or something else)
3. Normative changes are opt-in by both RAS and IdP
4. IdP AS Token Exchange contract can be extended with new protocol surface area (e.g `claims_required`) not defined in RFC 8693
6. Should `RAS Token Exchange to IdP` be in core spec or pushed to a future spec
7. Should claims discovery be defined in this spec or pushed to a future spec

comments.author: meghnadubey
comments.body:
> To allow IdPs to import a RAS's claim requirements at onboarding time rather than waiting for a runtime error, the RAS could advertise the claims it needs for JIT provisioning via its Authorization Server metadata (RFC 8414), using a new metadata parameter scoped to this profile (to avoid collision with base OAuth or other profiles).

I think this should become a part of the primary solution. If the IdP decides to rely on discovery metadata on JIT and records it in its RAS profile, it can apply polices and decide to include selective JIT claims that are standard OIDC claims beforehand in id-jag. The spec in this case is not prescribing a single solution(aud_sub/email), but letting the RAS publish its JIT requirements. And if the IdP chooses to add these claims(subject to policy), it may help avoid the extra round trips for most JIT cases. For the rest, `RAS token exchange to IdP` can be the fallback.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Need consensus on the following

1. The current spec is not sufficient for interoperable JIT scenarios with ID-JAG
2. JIT is an essential use case for cross-app access that needs a solution
3. Should ID-JAG or another spec define JIT for assertion grants and Token Exchange

The current proposal assumes JIT is not interoperable as-defined in current spec, its critical for cross-app, and it should be defined as part of ID-JAG.  The reason was the spec scope was Identity Assertion based Authorization Grant and JIT and claims requests are already a feature of SSO for similar reasons.  I also understand the value of narrowly scoping ID-JAG and pushing this to a companion spec.  

Once we agree on these questions we can hash out the details.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-insufficient-claims/

comments.author: yaron-zehavi
comments.body:
I think interoperable JIT is an essential requirement.
Reading the issue I reached the same security concern Aaron raised, and even more concerning is that IDP has no way of knowing if client's JIT claims request is based on RAS requirements. Client could over-ask and obtain an ID JAG revealing private information.

I think this should be solved and the solution:
- Should be metadata discovery based. For example a RAS can publish it's JIT required claims.
- An IDP can discover the audienced RAS' JIT claims, so client signaling would not be required (prevents unauthorized "step-ups" of requested data.
- The JIT claims should not be included in the ID JAG, rather provided to RAS using token introspection. This ensures data privacy.

The challenge that remains is whether claim names have the same meaning for IDP and RAS.
When Standard OIDC claims are used, the meaning is clear.
When custom claims are used, their meaning could conflict in different domains.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
The required claims may be contextual to the user, client, resource, tenant, etc.  A static claims list per RAS published in global metadata may not be sufficient.  IdPs already need tenant specific dictionaries for groups, roles, etc for example.   There may also be different claims needed for API access with ID-JAG vs traditional SSO.   Discovering the full set of claims needed for JIT that includes account profile, roles, entitlements, authorization, etc is a larger surface area than just static list of claims such as `claims_supported` in OIDC metadata.

OIDC already supports an open claims request mechanism https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#ClaimsParameter.  Entra ID already uses this with claims challenge using WWW-Authenticate challenges https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/claims-challenge?tabs=dotnet.   The insufficient claims challenge is modeled similarly https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-insufficient-claims/ as patterns that have already been deployed.

If we really want to solve for privacy, then an alternative solution would be a flow similar to https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-rosomakho-oauth-txn-challenge/ where a claims challenge can be signed an optionally encrypted by the RAS and carried back to the IdP.  I think this is overkill personally. 

The end-to-end solution will more than likely require the IdP to use SCIM/OpenID Provider Commands and potentially vendor-specific APIs to populate the attributes needed to JIT users across a wide range of app types, tenant models, etc.   A more generic app-boarding control plane like FastFed would be more suited to address this challenge I believe than public AS metadata.

comments.author: yaron-zehavi
comments.body:
Okay, but then to support dynamic sets of attributes required by RAS, while maintaining privacy and preventing unauthorized step-up, perhaps IDP should issue its ID-JAG with a default set of claims and if RAS if requires more, it shall make a token introspection request adding `required_claims` as request parameter..
RFC 7662 supports optional request parameters, IDP identifies the token as an ID JAG it issued and so perhaps dynamic claim negotiation could be performed directly between RAS and IDP, without failure signaling and without involving the client.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Can you elaborate on the flow you are thinking off.  I'm not following where token introspection fits.

comments.author: yaron-zehavi
comments.body:
With pleasure:

- Client requests IDP for ID JAG and obtains one with (IDP profiled) standard set of claims (e.g sub, name and email)
- Client presents ID JAG to RAS
- RAS validates and evaluates ID JAG, determines the token is valid but the identity claims are insufficient. (e.g: department & employee_number are required).
- RAS calls IDPs token introspection endpoint for the ID JAG and adds a required_claims request parameter: `required_claims=department%20employee_number`, with appropriate client authentication.
- IDP validates ID JAG, and that caller is the RAS the audience of the ID JAG.
- IDP evaluates the required claims and provides them over TLS in the token introspection response.

et voila!
Dynamic claims negotiation without relying on static metadata contracts, completely transparent to clients and without security risks from clients (unauthorized requests for more claims, privacy).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Thanks for elaboration it helps.

1) Is access token issuance blocked for the client while steps 4-6 are happening?  This will have scale issues for high volume RAS deployments. You would more than likely introduce a dependency on DTR and lots of polling.  Having an external network dependency during token issuance has known operational concerns.  
2) The ID-JAG is issued to the client and ideally bound to the client's key for proof-of-possession key.  The RAS is not the client the token was issued for.  How does the IdP know its the RAS making the introspection request in an interoperable way (the ID-JAG audience value doesn't match as CIMD url for the RAS as a client for example)? 
3) The IdP still needs a policy to determine whether the RAS can request specific claims. 
4) The IdP may not be accessible the the RAS.  The client is the only actor that needed to reach the IdP. 

Since the IdP still needs a policy to determine what claims can be requested for given subject/client/audience/resource tuple,   I feel like JWE encryption of the ID-JAG addresses the P0 for privacy concerns with all the complexity.  See https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/pull/102

This also starts to look like a token exchange by RAS for an access token for UserInfo endpoint that I mentioned in some channel (can't find it) which would mirror OIDC for getting claims in the backchannel.

comments.author: yaron-zehavi
comments.body:
Agree with the latency concerns but not sure how much they'll impact users as XAA flows run in the background, so perhaps better have client synch wait on the token exchange call than defer with DTR.

Disagree on points 3 & 4:

- IdP needs a per-RAS policy also in the original proposal, to process audience + required_claims pairs in the token exchange request.
- IdP needs to be accessible to RAS for obtaining jwks to validate the ID JAG.

Agree error signaling + JWE can solve all of this without RAS adding a network dependency.
If not opting for JWE for whatever reason, combining both my proposals could lower latency:

- IdP shall consider RAS published required claims profile when issuing ID JAG's, raising the chance they satisfy JIT requirements.
- RAS may dynamically request additional claims through introspection.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
> IdP needs a per-RAS policy also in the original proposal, to process audience + required_claims pairs in the token exchange request.

This was the significant bit.  The IdP will  always need policy for the subject/client/audience/resource tuple and a client can't obtain a token with claims the IdP didn't authorize as consent is owned by the IdP policy/administrator not the resource owner.   A client can't request claims that exceed the claim policy for the subject/client/audience/resource. JWE only addresses privacy concerns of preventing the client from introspecting additional claims.  The IdP policy is the claims ceiling.  Metadata can helps scale policy authoring/validation but doesn't change the need for the IdP to at runtime make a decision on what claims to issue for the request. 

Circling back on the open question for ID-JAG, should this spec define the signaling and claims request mechanism for JIT or should this be a separate spec and ID-JAG just needs to support JWE?  Should ID-JAG support OIDC scopes as way to request pre-defined claims similar to OIDC?

comments.author: yaron-zehavi
comments.body:
I think it would be valuable if the spec would support JIT claim negotiation for standard OIDC scopes or claims, as well as provide secure mechanisms to request and exchange them.
Support for custom claims I'd leave to profiles.

issues.title: Clarify cross-domain use restriction
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
> This specification is intended for cross-domain uses where the Client, Resource App, and Identity Provider are all in different trust domains. In particular, the Identity Provider MUST NOT issue access tokens in response to an ID-JAG it issued itself. Doing so could lead to unintentional broadening of the scope of authorization.

This should not preclude a single piece of software from being both an IdP and Resource AS.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
correct. crossing tenants for example is example of cross-domain for same software. 

Is there a use case that is driving the need to add this clarification?

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body: The open source IdP/AS [Athenz](https://techblog.lycorp.co.jp/ja/20260401a) implemented issuing ID-JAGs and also processing ID-JAGs and they were concerned that they had done something wrong after reading that sentence.

issues.title: Allow public client registration at the Resource Authorization Server when the client is confidential at the IdP and the ID-JAG is key-bound?
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
The current draft generally assumes confidential clients at the Resource Authorization Server (RAS), and the Security Considerations say that this specification `SHOULD` only be supported for confidential clients. The draft also notes in Cross-Domain Client ID Handling that requiring a confidential client at the RAS helps prevent the IdP from delegating access to any valid client at the RAS.

At the same time, the draft now defines proof-of-possession / key-binding for ID-JAG using `cnf` and DPoP. That raises a question about whether the spec should allow an explicit tradeoff here.

**Deployment model to discuss**

- The client is confidential at the IdP.
- The client is public at the RAS, or the RAS otherwise does not require confidential client authentication for this exchange.
- The client includes DPoP in the token exchange to the IdP.
- The IdP issues a key-bound ID-JAG with a `cnf` / `jkt`.
- The client presents DPoP when exchanging the ID-JAG at the RAS.
- The RAS verifies that the DPoP key matches the `cnf` in the ID-JAG.

**Why allow this**

- Credential lifecycle can be centralized at the IdP.
- The client does not need to maintain separate credentials with each RAS.
- This may be useful in ecosystems with many downstream RAS deployments.
- Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) helps address part of this problem when adopted, but it will not always be available immediately.
- This could make the deployment model possible until CIMD becomes more widely deployed.

**Tradeoff**

This is not equivalent to requiring a confidential client at the RAS.

What is preserved:

- Replay resistance for the ID-JAG, assuming the RAS requires proof-of-possession and validates `cnf` against the proof token.
- Stronger protection than an unconstrained bearer-style exchange.

What is reduced:

- The RAS no longer gets the same client-authentication assurance it gets from a confidential registration at the RAS.
- The anti-client-substitution property is weaker unless the spec explicitly defines how public-client identification is handled in this profile.

**Question**

Should the specification explicitly allow this tradeoff?

Possible direction:

- Keep confidential registration at the RAS as the recommended/default model.
- Allow RAS deployments to accept public clients for ID-JAG exchange when the ID-JAG is key-bound and the proof token presented to the RAS matches the `cnf`.
- Clarify that this does not require any RAS to support public clients.
- A RAS, or the administrator/operator of that RAS, can always decide to require confidential registration instead.
- In that sense, this change would make the model possible, not mandatory, until CIMD is more widely deployed.

If the spec does allow this, it would likely need explicit processing rules for this profile, for example:

- `cnf` in the ID-JAG is required.
- Proof-of-possession at the RAS is required.
- The proof key MUST match the `cnf` in the ID-JAG.
- The RAS SHOULD issue only sender-constrained access tokens in this case.
- The client identification / `client_id` matching rules need to be defined for public clients at the RAS.

The main question is whether the spec should permit this as an optional deployment tradeoff, while still allowing any RAS to require confidential registration.

comments.author: meghnadubey
comments.body:
Allowing public client with DPoP provides flexibility at the RAS, in case it is not already supporting CIMD, or wants to selectively support CIMD. This ventures into RAS policy, but I think the advantages are significant enough to add to the spec. 
CIMD may not always be implemented by the client, and manual client registration involves some effort for the client and IdP to maintain the external registration. I think even with the known downsides, public client with DPoP should be available as an option.

issues.title: Add `authorization_grant_profiles_supported` to client metadata too
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Clients should be able to advertise support for this profile via DCR/CIMD as well.

This would need a new section "Client Metadata" after "Authorization Server Metadata", and a new IANA registry section to add `authorization_grant_profiles_supported` and `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-profile:id-jag` to the [DCR registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/oauth-parameters/oauth-parameters.xhtml#client-metadata).

issues.title: ID-JAG standard claim change suggestions
issues.author: khosravian
issues.body:
Hi Everyone, 

I've been slowly reviewing the standard document and came across a couple of cases I wanted to bring up:

First:
>    resource:  OPTIONAL - The Resource Identifier (Section 2 of
      [RFC8707]) of the Resource Server (either a single URI or an array
      of URIs).

Can we change this claim description to always be an array of URIs? I understand the recommendation is very nit-picky, although it would be much easier for ID_JAG consumers to handle 'resource' claim validation if it's included.

Second: 
>    client_id:  REQUIRED - The client identifier of the OAuth 2.0
      [RFC6749] client at the Resource Authorization Server that will
      act on behalf of the resource owner (sub).  This identifier MAY be
      different that client identifier of the OAuth 2.0 client
      requesting an ID-JAG from the IdP Section 4.3 of [RFC8693] as it
      represents and independent client relationship to another
      Authorization Server in a different trust domain.  See Section 5
      for additional considerations.

I understand the purpose of this claim and it makes sense, although maintenance of these client_id's can become very cumbersome in large scale deployments, I envision the client_id should be manually set at the AS and there isn't any dynamic relationship between the AS and the Resource Authorization Server. Also perhaps dpop can be used to accomplish the same outcome.

I want to suggest to change the type from "REQUIRED" to "RECOMMENDED". The change would potentially help with the large scale maintenance issues.

Thanks,
Jamshid

comments.author: bc-pi
comments.body: On the second item, worth noting that the direction of #85 would reduce the usefulness of a `client_id` claim. Which might be further rational for not having it REQUIRED.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
fwiw [Client ID Metadata Document](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/) also solves the client ID management problem at scale.

As for the `resource` parameter, I recognize some programming languages don't like dynamically typed values, but I'm not sure that's enough of a reason to restrict this to always be an array.

comments.author: sdesen
comments.body: making client id optional would conflict with the 4.4.1 processing rules with dictate it must match the client authentication

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: @sdesen #85 has a proposal to relax that constraint for sender-constrained assertions.  There isn't consensus on the issue and there real security tradeoffs but advantages for deployability.

comments.author: khosravian
comments.body:
Thank you for your feedback everyone, 

@aaronpk regarding the `resource` change suggestion, i get it, it's a personal preference from a java developer perspective.

issues.title: Prior art for future revisions
issues.author: GoetzGW
issues.body:
Hi Aaron / Karl / Brian,

Bjørn Baunbæk and Götz Wehberg from the Gimel Foundation here. This is a constructive prior-art notification for any future revision of `draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant` (WG-adopted 25 August 2025; superseding `draft-parecki-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-05` of 2 July 2025).

The Gimel Foundation has published a body of open-core specifications on AI-agent authorization that we believe are directly relevant to - at least - three specific touch-points in the XAA surface as it is likely to evolve. We are filing this as a public-track companion to a direct authors-side note that has been sent off-list to the three of you in parallel.

Three concrete touch-points (not limited to these)
1. `subject_token` shape — PoA Credential as a candidate alongside OIDC ID Token and SAML assertion. Today XAA names the OIDC ID Token and the SAML assertion as the two assertions a client may exchange. The Gimel Power-of-Attorney (PoA) Credential defined in GiFo-RFC 0115 carries a structured mandate (principal, agent, scope, delegation chain, expiry, narrowing rules) and could be carried as a `subject_token` of a third explicitly-named type in a future companion document. This becomes useful the moment XAA needs to describe agent-acting-on-behalf-of-user as distinct from user-with-app, which the "coming soon: secure agent-to-agent delegation" line item in the Okta blueprint will at some point require.

2. Multi-hop scope narrowing — already specified in GiFo-RFC 0115 §3.7. RFC 0115 §3.7 specifies mandatory scope narrowing across multi-hop delegation chains: a sub-agent's credential can only narrow, never broaden, the parent's scope, and this is enforced cryptographically rather than by IdP policy lookup. This is the surface the Okta roadmap names as "secure agent-to-agent delegation" (announced 29 April 2026). When that work begins inside the OAuth WG, RFC 0115 §3.7 is published prior art.

3. Runtime PEP — already specified in GiFo-RFC 0117 §4. RFC 0117 §4 specifies a sixteen-check pre-action enforcement pipeline at the Policy Enforcement Point (scope boundaries, delegation-chain integrity, temporal validity, resource constraints, etc.) with a three-way decision model (PERMIT / DENY / CONSTRAIN — i.e., narrow the action to a subset of what was requested rather than refuse outright). This is the surface the Okta roadmap names as "Agent Gateway." RFC 0117 publishes April 2026; the substantive prior-art anchor for this primitive is also a priority of filed patents.

Requests for a future revision (or a companion document)
A Related Work / Informative Reference entry naming GiFo-RFC 0115 (PoA Credential), GiFo-RFC 0117 (PEP Interface) and beyond as the closest published prior-art surfaces for the three touch-points above, not limited to these.

What this is currently not
- Not an infringement assertion against XAA `-05` or its WG-adopted successor.
- Not a request to change the substantive normative content of XAA itself, which we currently read as architecturally complementary to GAuth.
- A contribution under IETF terms 

All relevant GiFo RFCs are licensed under Apache 2.0 (Specs) or MPL 2.0 (SDKs), both come together with the Legal Terms of the Gimel Foundation. Specs are at `https://github.com/Gimel-Foundation`. Happy to provide section-level pointers or take a call.

Thank you and kind regards!

Bjørn Baunbæk & Götz Wehberg, on behalf of Gimel Foundation

issues.title: How can a Resource Authorization Server recognize an ID-JAG when it is configured with SAML SSO
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
When a Resource Authorization Server is configured to the enterprise IdP with SAML for SSO, the values currently in the ID-JAG are not able to be mapped to their SAML equivalents.

For example, the Resource AS might recognize a SAML issuer like `https://example.com/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346` and receive SAML NameIds that are a username or email address. An ID-JAG will contain an OIDC issuer URL like `https://tenant123.example.com/` and subject identifiers that are a random string. (there is no guarantee the SAML issuer and OIDC issuer domain names have anything in common.)

When a Resource AS is configured for SAML SSO, what are the options for how it can map the ID-JAG values to the SAML SSO connection? As far as I can tell there are a couple options for the issuer:

* No change to the ID-JAG, require that the customer manually add the OIDC issuer URL into their SAML SSO configuration. This provides the AS the association between the SAML issuer and OIDC issuer.
* Include the SAML issuer in the ID-JAG somewhere.

For the user ID question, the options would be:

* Send whatever value the SAML NameId would have been in the ID-JAG `sub` (this is currently allowed according to [section 3.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-03.html#section-3.1) because it would be "the same as the subject identifier used in an Identity Assertion for the Resource Authorization Server as a Relying Party for Single Sign-On (SSO)")
* Send the SAML NameId as a new claim in the ID-JAG

If we go with adding new claims to the ID-JAG, the question becomes whether these should be SAML-specific claims or something generic, e.g.

* `saml_issuer` and `saml_nameid`
* `alt_issuer` and `alt_sub`

### Minimal Changed Example ID-JAG

```
{
  "typ": "oauth-id-jag+jwt"
}
.
{
  "jti": "9e43f81b64a33f20116179",
  "iss": "https://acme.idp.example",
  "sub": "user@idp.example",                  /* assuming email addresses were sent as SAML NameId */
  "aud": "https://acme.chat.example/",
  "client_id": "f53f191f9311af35",
  "exp": 1311281970,
  "iat": 1311280970,
  "resource": "https://acme.chat.example/api",
  "scope": "chat.read chat.history"
}
.
signature
```

### Example ID-JAG with New Claims

```
{
  "typ": "oauth-id-jag+jwt"
}
.
{
  "jti": "9e43f81b64a33f20116179",
  "iss": "https://acme.idp.example",
  "sub": "U019488227",
  "alt_iss": "https://idp.example/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346",
  "alt_sub": "user@idp.example",
  "aud": "https://acme.chat.example/",
  "client_id": "f53f191f9311af35",
  "exp": 1311281970,
  "iat": 1311280970,
  "resource": "https://acme.chat.example/api",
  "scope": "chat.read chat.history"
}
.
signature
```

comments.author: dlozlla
comments.body:
We don't currently configure any issuer on SAML connections, but the certificate with the public key we use to validate the SAML Response. In that regard, our initial intention is to add the option to add an OIDC issuer as part of the SAML connection configuration. I think in that regard we wouldn't really need to receive an `alt_iss`.

For the user ID issue, we do need to receive the same value we would receive in the SAM response for the same user, so we would need those two values to come in the `id-jag` if they are different in SAML and OIDC spaces for the IdP.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
These interop gaps were a key driver for [SAML 2.0 to OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0 Migration Profile](https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-connect-saml-migration/draft-mcguinness-saml-oidc-migration-profile.html) which is focused on the Client to IDP AS and not RAS. 

# SAML Issuer

My draft defines metadata for

- SAML Metadata publishes the AS Issuer Metadata URI
- AS Issuer Metadata published the SAML Metadata URI

This forms a bidirectional binding between the SAML IdP entity and the OAuth issuer that can be resolved using either protocol.

The draft does enable these values to be per-client for example for multi-tenant issuers with client registration overrides but unfortunately there isn't an existing channel outside of DCR access token to fetch client registration metadata.   There isn't a spec for per-client AS metadata (yet, but there should be one day) that would be convenient for this gap.

> When a Resource AS is configured for SAML SSO, what are the options for how it can map the ID-JAG values to the SAML SSO connection? As far as I can tell there are a couple options for the issuer:
> 
> No change to the ID-JAG, require that the customer manually add the OIDC issuer URL into their SAML SSO configuration. This provides the AS the association between the SAML issuer and OIDC issuer.
> Include the SAML issuer in the ID-JAG somewhere.
> 

Passing the SAML Issuer in the ID-JAG can be useful as a compatibility hint, but it is dangerous if the RAS uses it to establish trust dynamically. The core security issue is that the value is attacker-influenced until the ID-JAG has already been validated under a trusted JWT issuer.

The safe rule is:

The SAML Issuer in the ID-JAG can help select an existing SAML trust relationship only after the RAS has already validated the ID-JAG iss, signature, aud, expiration, and client binding against configured ID-JAG trust. It must not be used to decide whether the ID-JAG issuer is trusted in the first place.

I don't think its wise to include the SAML issuer in the ID-JAG for this reason. 

# SAML Subject NameID

SAML Name ID in my draft is addressed via defined mapping to an ID Token or Token Introspection (https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-connect-saml-migration/draft-mcguinness-saml-oidc-migration-profile.html#name-subject-identifier-mapping).   I don't think this solution works for the RAS role with the ID-JAG which is downstream. 

I think for scenarios where the identifier is not mutable, it can easily be passed as the `sub` of the ID-JAG with similar rules as https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-connect-saml-migration/draft-mcguinness-saml-oidc-migration-profile.html#name-subject-identifier-mapping.  For scenarios where it is mutable, then its OK to define a new claim.  I do wonder how many these scenarios its email which is already a claim ID-JAG supports.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
In the [definition of the ID-JAG claims](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-03.html#section-3.1), it says 

> The identifier MUST be the same as the subject identifier used in an Identity Assertion for the Resource Authorization Server as a Relying Party for Single Sign-On (SSO)

So for the Resource App, when the SAML NameId is configured as the email address, we've been interpreting this as the `sub` in the ID-JAG should be the email address.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: I was over-indexing on OIDCs normative rule around sub claim. ID-JAG can have a more relaxed take. There are side effects for subject resolution and JIT that we will need to document. I would still prefer that sub is RECOMMENDED to be immutable.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body: Are there any cases of a SAML NameId having attributes other than the string value? That might be enough of a reason to move the SAML NameId into its own claim in the ID-JAG and create a definition of how to represent those in JSON.

comments.author: gffletch
comments.body: According to this [SAML V2.0 Subject Identifier Attribute Profile v1.0](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml-subject-id-attr/v1.0/cs01/saml-subject-id-attr-v1.0-cs01.html) there may be some SAML deployments that don't use `NameID` at all. I don't know if this is a common deployment model or not.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
SAML Subject NameID is a string but it also may carry semantic qualifiers and metadata attributes such as:

- Format
- NameQualifier
- SPNameQualifier
- SPProvidedID

As @gffletch indicated, the spec also doesn't require NameID but from my experience its required for most of SaaS based deployments.  

There is a lot of surface area to define mappings and interoperability requirements.   You can get a taste of the complexity https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-connect-saml-migration/draft-mcguinness-saml-oidc-migration-profile.html#name-subject-identifier-mapping

One idea which as originally proposed in this issue was to adopt `sub_id` from secevents/SSF.

https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/issues/51#issuecomment-3398407476

We could define a new `format` for an SAML NameID 

Example ID-JAG:
```
{
  "iss": "https://tenant123.example.com/",
  "sub": "00u7abc123random",
  "aud": "https://resource-as.example.com/",
  "client_id": "client-123",
  "exp": 1715800000,
  "iat": 1715799700,
  "sub_id": {
    "format": "saml-nameid",
    "issuer": "https://example.com/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346",
    "nameid": "foo@example.com",
    "nameid_format": "urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress",
    "sp_name_qualifier": "https://resource.example.com/saml/sp"
  }
}
```

I would make only these required:

```
{
  "format": "saml-nameid",
  "issuer": "https://example.com/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346",
  "nameid": "foo@example.com"
}
```

And make the SAML qualifiers optional:

```
{
  "format": "saml-nameid",
  "issuer": "https://example.com/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346",
  "nameid": "foo@example.com",
  "nameid_format": "urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:persistent",
  "name_qualifier": "https://example.com/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346",
  "sp_name_qualifier": "https://resource.example.com/saml/sp",
  "sp_provided_id": "local-sp-provided-id"
}
```

The ID-JAG with still need a `sub` so we would still need to define that but  this works because RFC 9493 already says `sub_id` can identify the JWT subject using a different identifier namespace from the JWT iss/sub which seems to match the use case here.  

Spec text shape:

`saml-nameid` Subject Identifier Format

The `saml-nameid` Subject Identifier Format identifies a subject using a SAML NameID value within the context of a SAML issuer.

A Subject Identifier in this format MUST contain:

* `format`: The value `saml-nameid`.
* `issuer`: A JSON string containing the SAML issuer/entityID.
* `nameid`: A JSON string containing the SAML NameID value.

A Subject Identifier in this format MAY contain:

* `nameid_format`: A JSON string containing the SAML NameID Format URI.
* `name_qualifier`: A JSON string containing the SAML NameQualifier value.
* `sp_name_qualifier`: A JSON string containing the SAML SPNameQualifier value.
* `sp_provided_id`: A JSON string containing the SAML SPProvidedID value.

Then add ID-JAG processing text:

When the Resource Authorization Server resolves users by SAML NameID, the IdP Authorization Server MAY include a `sub_id` claim using the `saml-nameid` Subject Identifier Format. The `sub_id` claim identifies the same subject as
the ID-JAG `sub` claim, but in the SAML subject namespace used by the Resource Authorization Server for SSO.

The Resource Authorization Server MAY use `sub_id` for subject resolution when it supports the indicated Subject Identifier Format.

Security guardrails:

The Resource Authorization Server MUST NOT use the `sub_id.issuer` value to establish trust in the ID-JAG issuer. The ID-JAG MUST first be validated using the `iss` claim, signature, audience, expiration, and client binding
according to this specification.

The Resource Authorization Server MUST use a `saml-nameid` `sub_id` only when the validated ID-JAG issuer is explicitly associated with the SAML issuer identified by `sub_id.issuer` through local configuration or trusted
federation metadata.

The IdP Authorization Server MUST include a `saml-nameid` `sub_id` only when the SAML NameID identifies the same subject as the ID-JAG `sub` claim for the target Resource Authorization Server.

I would also soften the current “sub MUST be the same as the SSO subject” language. It does not hold cleanly across OIDC and SAML. Better:

The `sub` claim identifies the End-User in the subject namespace of the ID-JAG issuer. When the Resource Authorization Server uses a different subject namespace for SSO, such as a SAML NameID namespace, the ID-JAG MAY include
`sub_id` to carry the SSO subject identifier. When both `sub` and `sub_id` are present, they MUST identify the same End-User.

That avoids forcing an impossible SAML NameID-to-JWT sub equality while still preserving the security invariant that both identifiers refer to the same user.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body: Yeah this makes sense to me. I like that it keeps the `iss`+`sub` value cleanly in the OIDC side of things, and also gives people a way to slowly map SAML user IDs to their corresponding OIDC user IDs.

comments.author: meghnadubey
comments.body: I agree with this approach of adding a complex claim that adds format specifier. It provides enough context and includes info on how to interpret the claim.

issues.title: Mention OpenID Connect scopes in the Token Exchange request explicitly
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Currently there is no mention of whether OpenID Connect scopes are allowed or not in the [Token Exchange step](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04.html#section-4.3) of the flow.

The text says 

> The space-separated list of scopes at the Resource Server that is being requested.

and OpenID Connect scopes are meant for client consumption, not resource server consumption, so it's kind of implied that they should not be accepted in the Token Exchange request.

Thoughts are welcome about which direction to go, but in either case we should mention that either they are acceptable in the request or they must not be included in the request.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: If there a mechanism to address #83 then I'm included to keep these scopes restricted to OIDC semantics of ID Token and/or Access Token and not ID-JAG as there is other solutions to get claims into the ID-JAG.  Without a solution to #83 then folks will want a way to get additional user claims into the ID-JAG based on the token exchange request which would lead them to re-using OIDC scopes.

issues.title: Should SAML->RT->ID-JAG flow suggest or require the `email` scope?
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Currently the spec says the client MUST request the `openid offline_access` scopes when exchanging the SAML assertion for refresh token.

It is likely, but not guaranteed, that the SAML assertion that the client has would already include the email address. (SAML can be configured to return opaque values for the `NameId`, and there is no guarantee the IdP would be configured to send an `email` attribute.)

If the SAML assertion did not have the email, you could argue the client should request the email scope because the ID-JAG will be visible to the client and would contain information beyond what is in the SAML assertion.

However, the purpose of including the `email` in the ID-JAG is for the benefit of the Resource AS, when it looks up users by email address from the SAML assertion. This behavior isn't necessarily known by the client, since it's about the relationship between the Resource AS and IdP.

So the question is whether we want to keep the text as is with the `email` claim being optional, or aim for better interoperability by suggesting/requiring that the client request the `email` scope.

Also note that if the IdP includes the `sub_id` property with the SAML NameId values, then the Resource AS likely won't need to rely on the `email` claim at all.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
This seems related to #99  and #83.   The lack of interop mechanism for a client to know what claims and needed and how to request them.  I don't think it makes sense to make `email` claim required as it's deployment specific.  Same with requiring a client to request `email` scope.  Its perfectly valid for a deployment to only use sub and sub_id and not email.  

The IdP AS isn't limited to minting claims in the ID-JAG that were only present in the subject_token.  Why can't the IdP AS make the decision to always send the email claim to a given RAS?

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
> The IdP AS isn't limited to minting claims in the ID-JAG that were only present in the subject_token.

Technically true, my thought there was along the privacy lines. If the client doesn't request `email`, but the IdP returns `email` in the ID-JAG, the client learns more than needed about the user. It's not really a concern in the enterprise scenario, but could be in the consumer scenarios. Maybe it doesn't matter because if the IdP is concerned about revealing info to the client it should always just not return that info even if the client requested it.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: I would prefer to keep this as deployment-specific for now and support something more generic for claims requests with #83.   I also think we should make it clear that JWE could be used by encrypting ID-JAG with RAS public key to address privacy concerns similar to ID-Token.  There many be other claims besides email that are PII and may need encryption for some deployments.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: PR https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/pull/102 for optional JWE support

issues.title: How can a client request a specific `aud_tenant`?
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
We have `aud_tenant` defined as an ID-JAG claim as follows:

> aud_tenant:
> OPTIONAL - A JSON string that represents a Resource Authorization Server tenant identifier. This claim is only included when the Resource Authorization Server is multi-tenant and the IdP knows the tenant identifier.

For the case where the IdP and Resource AS do not use tenanted identifiers, and there are multiple copies of the app behind the Resource AS installed in the IdP, this claim is the only thing that can identify the app.

How can a client request a particular app? We didn't want to add `aud_tenant` as a claim to the Token Exchange request. We do have text in the `audience` parameter of token exchange:

> IdP Authorization Servers MAY also support implementation-specific audience values, such as URNs, that identify pre-established trust relationships with Resource Authorization Servers. When such a value is used, the IdP Authorization Server resolves it to the corresponding Resource Authorization Server identifier and issues the ID-JAG with that identifier in the aud claim.

I think two things need to happen:

* We should define a standardized method for referencing `aud_tenant` here
* Update the last part to "...resolves it to the corresponding Resource Authorization Server identifier and issues the ID-JAG with that identifier in the aud claim and aud_tenant"

Thoughts?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Can you provide a concrete example of the deployment where you have shared client registration for each "application" that also shares a common authorization server (`aud`) but is not a tenant in the shared authorization server and the client knows this value for XAA?  

The original thinking was that something like https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-token-xchg-target-svc-disco/ would be needed for a client to discover IdP-specific identifiers for different targets.

It will have to be flexible to accommodate most RAS.

Also a complex `aud_tenant/context` will be required to solve this problem. The complex claim can follow the format:value model of sub_id, to accommodate the full RAS specific context set by the admin for the RAS apps in the IdP. 

Example:
```
"aud_context": {
  "format": "ras_context",
  "accountId": "gytgi7ygho80",
  "domain": "dev.acme",
}
```

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Can you provide more concrete example? I am not clear why this metadata can't be on discovery endpoints with then a opaque identifier used as the audience in the token exchange request. 

> Also a complex aud_tenant/context will be required to solve this problem. 

I think this already past the interoperable surface area and better solved with custom claims for the RAS.   I fail to see why `aud_context` with yet another extensible dictionary solves interop vs just having custom claims for the RAS.   

Finally how is this solved for SSO?

comments.body:
> I think this already past the interoperable surface area and better solved with custom claims for the RAS

Custom claims will also solve RAS specific requirements. Because, the RAS context may not be limited to tenant and there could be other identifiers that work alone or in conjunction for user authorization.

Example: If the IdP has two apps available for the subject, for accessing same resource but different env/domains, dev and staging, and the audience and resource is the same, there is no request parameter that can help distinguish between a id-jag resource access request, for dev/staging. So there is no way to resolve what should be set in the `aud_tenant`.

comments.body:
Why aren't `dev` and `staging` tenants in your example?  I assume you are referring to `dev` and `staging` as 2 instances of the resource app the customer is using as `dev` and `staged` for their deployment that are managed by the same IdP and not different environments of the resource app (which I wouldn't expect to share the same AS).  

Again, can we provide a full end-to-end scenario for this issue and describe how SSO works for the deployment.

comments.author: meghnadubey
comments.body:
> Why aren't dev and staging tenants in your example? I assume you are referring to dev and staging as 2 instances of the resource app the customer is using as dev and staged for their deployment that are managed by the same IdP

That is correct. In this case dev and staging are tenants. But tenant may not be enough for all RAS, so custom claim maybe needed.

With SSO into the resource app, the user consent and SSO context should provide enough info to the RAS to authorize granular access. But in the case of `identity-assertion-authz-grant` there is a level of indirection, where the subject has only SSO'ed into the requesting app and based on that, requests for id-jag for RAS, that requires interpretation to resolve which resource app's context should be sent in the id-jag claim.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
I updated editor's draft of https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-token-xchg-target-svc-disco/draft-mcguinness-token-xchg-target-svc-disco.html#name-multi-tenant-target-service to include additional discovery metadata and have a logical identifier for the audience+tenant or client relationship. issues.title: Token Exchange response lacks signal for sender-constraint binding when token_type is "N_A"
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Gap

OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693 §2.2.1) requires the `token_type` response parameter to be `N_A` when the issued token is not used directly as an access token, which is the case for an ID-JAG. This removes the signal that elsewhere in OAuth tells the client which sender-constraint binding (if any) was applied to the issued token. RFC 9449 (DPoP), for example, uses `token_type: "DPoP"` for normal access token responses, but that path is not available for ID-JAGs.

Today the client's only path to detect sender-constraint binding on an ID-JAG is to inspect the ID-JAG itself for an RFC 7800 `cnf` claim. This works for JWS ID-JAGs but fails in two cases:

1. **Encrypted ID-JAGs.** With the JWE-encryption support added in #102, the inner JWS is encrypted to the Resource Authorization Server and is opaque to the client.

2. **Opaque issued tokens generally.** Any future profile that issues opaque tokens via Token Exchange faces the same problem.

The current draft acknowledges this in the DPoP section by recommending the client inspect the ID-JAG for `cnf`, with a caveat (added in #102) that the inspection is impossible when the ID-JAG is encrypted. The result is that a client requesting DPoP binding cannot detect a silent downgrade by the IdP Authorization Server when encryption is in use.

## Why this matters

Without a Token Exchange response-level signal, an IdP Authorization Server that silently fails to apply sender-constraining (by error or by misbehavior) can downgrade the issued ID-JAG without the client noticing. The detection path that exists for unencrypted ID-JAGs (client introspects the JWS) is unavailable for encrypted ID-JAGs, and it never existed for opaque tokens.

This gap is not specific to ID-JAG. Any Token Exchange flow that issues a sender-constrained token where `token_type: "N_A"` is required has the same problem.

## Possible solution

A small extension to RFC 8693 that adds an optional `cnf` parameter to the Token Exchange response. The value reuses the RFC 7800 confirmation structure (`jkt` for DPoP, `x5t#S256` for mTLS, etc.). The authorization server includes it when sender-constraining was applied; the client validates it against the key or certificate it provided in the request. Absence (when binding was expected) is treated as downgrade.

Sketched as an individual draft for working group feedback:

https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-oauth-token-exchange-cnf/draft-mcguinness-oauth-token-exchange-cnf.html

If adopted, the ID-JAG draft could simplify its current DPoP and encryption text by deferring to the response parameter rather than prescribing client-side token introspection.

## Asking for

Feedback on whether a Token Exchange response parameter is the right shape for closing this gap, and whether the sketched draft covers the requirements ID-JAG needs.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: I submitted https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-token-exchange-cnf/ to address this gap, linking here for reference

issues.title: What should this spec say about DPoP server-provided nonces and replay protection?
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
Is there anything this spec needs to say about server-provided nonces? 

* [authorization server provided nonce](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449#name-authorization-server-provid)
* [resource server provided nonce](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449#name-resource-server-provided-no)
* [replay considerations](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449#name-dpop-proof-replay)

My suspicion is that there isn't anything unique to this spec that would dictate whether these are required, and that they are still going to be up to implementations to decide whether are necessary. But it at least wouldn't hurt to mention these mechanisms for a reader of this spec who isn't familiar with the details of DPoP.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Agree with your instinct. DPoP nonces and proof-replay are RFC 9449 mechanics that this spec doesn't need to mandate or constrain. 

There are two things I think might be worth saying explicitly for a reader who isn't deep in DPoP

1. The AS-provided-nonce mechanism (RFC 9449 §8) applies at two endpoints in this flow: the IdP's Token Exchange endpoint and the RAS's JWT-bearer token endpoint. Each maintains its own nonce state; nothing crosses between them.
2. DPoP proof replay protection (RFC 9449 §11.1) is per-recipient. `htm`/`htu` ensure each proof is scoped to a single endpoint, so the IdP and RAS track DPoP `jti` independently.
