issues.title: Usage of "resource" request parameter incompatible with oauth-identity-chaining
issues.author: randomstuff
issues.body:
oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant is expected to be a profile of [identity chaining](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining/):

> Identity Chaining intentionally leaves many details unspecified in order to support multiple use cases. **This specification profiles it [Identity Chaining]** […]

However, their definition of the `resource` parameter in the token Exchange Request is incompatible:

* For identity chaining, this identifies the *authorization server* for trust domain B (i.e. the *resource authorization server*)
* For identity assertion authz grant, this identified the *resource server*

***

In identity chaining, we have:

> Token Exchange Request
>
> […]
>
> resource, URI of **authorization server** for trust domain B

In oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant:

> The Client makes a Token Exchange [[RFC8693](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693)] request to the IdP Authorization Server's Token Endpoint with the following parameters:
>
> […]
>
> resource: OPTIONAL - The Resource Identifier of the **Resource Server** as defined in [Section 2](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707#section-2) of [[RFC8707](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707)].

***

I would claim oauth-identity-chaining is more consistent with the definition of `resource` because as per RFC 8693, they are supposed to have the [same semantic meaning](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693#name-request).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Identity Chaining draft-19 (latest) says

> One of resource or audience is REQUIRED to indicate the intended authorization server in trust domain B.

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining-16.html#section-2.3.1

My read was ID-JAG profile MAY use `audience` to identify the RAS in token exchange request parameter and allow `resource`  to be the Resource Identifier of the Resource Server.  ID-JAG does allow an IdP specific identifier for the RAS which may be considered as a logical identifier.  

@aaronpk what is your take here?

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
I had been similarly thinking of the identity chaining definition as using the `audience` to identify the RAS freeing up the `resource` for other purposes. 

The Token Exchange definition of the terms does not limit the parameters to identify the authorization server, it says "target service or resource", and a "service" can be the combination of the resource AS and RS.

issues.title: Standardize error code for "user does not have a license" - today we get `invalid_grant`
issues.author: pcarleton
issues.body:
On the final leg of the ID-JAG flow, we often get back `invalid_grant` when a user does not have a license (i.e. it's a 100 person company, and only 50 people have a Figma license). This causes problems because it's difficult to know when to retry and what to tell the user for how to get access to the app.  `invalid_grant` is indistinguishable from a misconfiguration.

Related, but separate issue from discussion, is the user might have a license in the resource server, but it's not configured in the IdP.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
A see a couple path are available for this scenario

1. Since this is an entitlement issue and not specific to ID-JAG processing the RAS could return `access_denied` error instead of `invalid_grant`.  This would enable the client to know that the requesting a new ID-JAG won't resolve the issue and the end-user needs to remediate using a company specific access request approval process. 
2. The RAS could return `interaction_required` per draft spec https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-parecki-oauth-jwt-grant-interaction-response/.  This would enable the client to switch to front channel to remediate the error such as kicking off an access request workflow from the resource app if the app supports a requestable denial pattern. 
3. If the entitlement is a claim from the IdP, the RAS could challenge the client for the required claim per draft https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-insufficient-claims/.  This is the scenario #83 issue is tracking.

In short, an end-user not being entitled to an app but be granted "SSO" by the IdP is a scenario that already exists today.  The delta is they land on a error screen in the browser at the app that has an error message and its up to the end-user to know the process to request access. 

@aaronpk if you agree that `access_denied` is valid for this scenario then I can get a PR up that clarifies this. 

As for the IdP, I submitted https://github.com/aaronpk/draft-parecki-oauth-jwt-grant-interaction-response/issues/1 to enable `interaction_required` to also be supported for Token Exchange.  The IdP should also be able to return `access_denied` for authorization scenarios where the client+user are not granted access to the RAS.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body: Yeah `access_denied` feels like the right error code to use here.

issues.title: Relax confidential client requirement when the ID Token is key-bound (OpenID Connect Key Binding 1.0)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Context

The current draft says in Security Considerations that this specification SHOULD only be supported for confidential clients, and Cross-Domain Client ID Handling notes that requiring a confidential client at the Resource Authorization Server helps prevent the IdP from delegating access to any valid client at the Resource Authorization Server.

Issue #85 asks whether this constraint can be relaxed when the ID-JAG itself is key-bound via `cnf`/DPoP, on the theory that proof-of-possession at the RAS provides an alternative to confidential client authentication at the RAS.

This issue proposes a related but distinct relaxation, one layer earlier: when the ID Token used as the `subject_token` is key-bound via OpenID Connect Key Binding 1.0 (https://openid.github.io/connect-key-binding/main.html), the authentication assurance for the client is anchored in the ID Token itself, and the confidential-client requirement can be reconsidered on that basis.

## Proposal

Allow the Client at the IdP to be a public client, or otherwise not required to present confidential client credentials at the Token Exchange endpoint, when all of the following hold:

- The `subject_token` is a key-bound ID Token per OpenID Connect Key Binding 1.0.
- The IdP validates the key binding of the ID Token per that spec.
- The IdP issues a key-bound ID-JAG whose `cnf` is derived from (or otherwise chained to) the ID Token's binding key or an explicit DPoP proof presented alongside.
- The Client presents proof-of-possession when redeeming the ID-JAG at the Resource Authorization Server, and the RAS validates the `cnf` against that proof per the existing DPoP processing rules.

The Resource Authorization Server-side confidential requirement would remain a deployment choice as discussed in #85; this issue focuses on the IdP-side Token Exchange step where the ID Token's key binding is the anchoring credential.

## How this relates to #85

- **#85** is about the RAS accepting public clients when the ID-JAG is key-bound at the RAS boundary. The anchoring credential there is the ID-JAG's `cnf` plus a proof presented to the RAS.
- **This issue** is about the IdP accepting a non-confidential client at Token Exchange when the ID Token itself is key-bound. The anchoring credential is the ID Token's own binding.

They can be adopted independently or together. Together, they enable an end-to-end model where the client's device (or the client's attestation-provided key) carries authentication assurance from SSO issuance through ID-JAG issuance to access token exchange, without requiring the client to maintain separate confidential credentials at either authorization server.

## Tradeoffs

Preserved:
- Sender-constraint on the ID Token, ID-JAG, and (if the RAS opts in) the access token.
- Prevention of casual replay by parties without the binding key.

Reduced or requiring explicit spec handling:
- Anti-substitution properties that rely on confidential client authentication at the IdP need to be reproved via the key-binding chain. Specifically: how the IdP validates that the Client presenting the ID Token is the same party the ID Token was issued to (this is exactly what OpenID Connect Key Binding covers, but the ID-JAG draft would need to say so and reference it).
- The Client's `client_id` at the IdP for Token Exchange still needs to be identified; the ID Token's `azp`/`aud` are the natural candidates, but the draft would need to state this normatively for the public-client-plus-key-bound case.

## Asking for

Feedback on whether this relaxation belongs in the base spec, or in a separate profile that stacks with #85's relaxation. If the working group is broadly comfortable with the direction, I'm happy to PR the required processing rules (validation, `client_id` derivation, cross-referencing OpenID Connect Key Binding 1.0).

issues.title: Architectural Conflict in Gateway / Proxy Topology with Public Clients (Section 4.3.3 Audience Check)
issues.author: leleueri
issues.body:
## Problem Summary In emerging **Agentic AI / Model Context Protocol (MCP)** architectures, a public client (e.g., a CLI tool or local agent) connects to a central API Gateway/Proxy, which then proxies requests to upstream services protected by distinct Resource Authorization Servers (AS). Under the current rules of `draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant` (Section 4.3.3), this multi-hop topology cannot legally execute the ID-JAG Token Exchange because: 1. The **Public Client** is the subject/audience of the initial OpenID Connect ID Token, but cannot (and should not) perform the ID-JAG Token Exchange. 2. The **Gateway** is the confidential client performing the Token Exchange, but its `client_id` fails the mandatory `aud` validation check against the ID Token presented in the request. --- ## Topology Overview ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor User participant Agent as Public Client
(AI Agent / CLI) participant IdP as Enterprise IdP participant Gateway as MCP Gateway
(Confidential Client) participant UpstreamAS as Upstream AS
(Resource AS) User->>Agent: Initiate action Agent->>IdP: OIDC Auth (PKCE) IdP-->>Agent: ID Token (aud = Agent client_id)
& Gateway Access Token Agent->>Gateway: Request tool call + ID Token Note over Gateway,IdP: ID-JAG Token Exchange Blocked Gateway->>IdP: Token Exchange Request
(subject_token = Agent ID Token) IdP--xGateway: ❌ REJECTED (Section 4.3.3)
aud (Agent) != client_id (Gateway) opt If Exchange Succeeded Gateway->>UpstreamAS: JWT-Bearer Redemption (ID-JAG) UpstreamAS-->>Gateway: Upstream Access Token end ``` 1. **Client Setup:** An AI coding agent acts as a public client (native/CLI app, PKCE, no client secret) and authenticates at the enterprise IdP. 2. **Initial Tokens:** As per OpenID Connect Core, the issued ID Token's `aud` claim is set to the agent's own `client_id`. In the same flow, the agent receives an access token scoped for an **MCP Gateway**. 3. **Gateway Aggregation:** The Gateway aggregates multiple upstream MCP servers. Each upstream server is protected by its own Resource Authorization Server (AS) that independently trusts the enterprise IdP. 4. **Target Flow (ID-JAG):** Per ID-JAG, to call an upstream server, the Gateway needs to redeem an access token by first calling Token Exchange (`grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`) at the IdP to obtain an ID-JAG (`aud = upstream_AS`), then executing a JWT-Bearer grant (`RFC 7523`) at that AS. --- ## Specification Conflict ### 1. Section 4.3.3 Processing Rules Violation Section 4.3.3 (*IdP Token Exchange Processing Rules*) states: > *"When the subject_token presented in the Token Exchange call is an identity assertion (ID Token), the IdP MUST validate the assertion and MUST validate that the audience of the assertion (e.g., the aud claim of the ID Token or SAML Audience) matches the client_id of the client authentication of the request."* In the Gateway topology, this requirement creates a deadlock: * **The Agent cannot call Token Exchange:** * The agent's `client_id` matches the ID Token `aud`, but the agent does not know which upstream AS/audience a specific MCP tool call will require dynamically. * The agent is a **public client**, whereas Section 4 explicitly notes: *"This specification SHOULD only be supported for confidential clients."* * Giving public clients direct capability to mint cross-domain assertions breaches principle-of-least-privilege boundaries. * **The Gateway cannot call Token Exchange:** * The Gateway is a **confidential client** and knows which upstream AS to target. * However, when the Gateway authenticates the Token Exchange request using its own `client_id`, the IdP **MUST reject** the call because the ID Token's `aud` contains the Agent's `client_id`, not the Gateway's `client_id`. --- ## Questions & Possible Paths Forward 1. **Role of RFC 8693 Actor Tokens / Identity Chaining:** Should ID-JAG explicitly address delegation/proxy patterns where the Gateway acts as an intermediary (e.g., utilizing `actor_token` [RFC 8693]) to relax the strict 1:1 `aud == authenticated_client_id` requirement for confidential proxies? 2. **Public Client + Gateway/Proxy Guidance:** As Agentic/MCP and API Gateway patterns become mainstream, is there an intended profile or recommended flow where an enterprise IdP allows a trusted confidential gateway to exchange a public client's ID Token on their behalf? I would appreciate the Working Group's perspective on whether this topology is considered out-of-scope, or if the specification could accommodate intermediate confidential proxies.

comments.author: 0xbrainkid
comments.body:
This topology feels worth handling explicitly because it shows up in MCP gateways and agent tool routers: the runtime that starts the user session is often not the component that can safely know or mint every downstream audience.

One way to keep the security boundary intact is to make the gateway exchange produce evidence of delegated authority rather than treating the public client's ID token as if it were simply addressed to the gateway. In practice I would want the resulting assertion or token exchange record to bind:

- subject user / initiating public client
- confidential gateway identity
- requested downstream audience
- actor/delegation chain
- tool or resource scope being requested
- policy version / decision time
- expiry and revocation context

That would let an upstream AS verify "this gateway is acting for this user/client, for this audience and purpose, under a fresh policy decision" without giving the public client broad cross-domain minting power or weakening the audience check into a generic bearer-token pass-through.

From the SATP / AgentFolio side, the important part is auditability across hops: if an autonomous agent action later needs a receipt, the authority chain should be reconstructable without trusting the agent runtime's own log summary. An explicit proxy/delegation profile here would help downstream tool protocols avoid inventing incompatible patterns around the same gap.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Extending ID-JAG to support public clients is an open topic. Related discussions:

- https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/issues/85 (public client at RAS with key-bound ID-JAG)
- https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/issues/113 (key-bound ID Token, relaxed client auth)

Forwarding the public client's ID Token to the gateway to present as its own `subject_token` is discouraged. The gateway is not the audience, and ID Tokens are not designed for cross-audience or cross-domain presentation. Section 4.3.3's audience check enforces that principle.

That leaves two directions worth exploring for your topology.

## Option A: Cross-client identity with `azp`

Model on Google's cross-client identity (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/cross-client-identity). The IdP is configured with one or more agent-gateway trust relationships. When the agent authenticates, the ID Token is issued with `aud=gateway` (or an array of eligible gateways) and `azp=agent`. The agent forwards the ID Token to the gateway; the transport mechanism between agent and gateway is outside the scope of ID-JAG. The gateway, acting as a confidential client, authenticates to the IdP at the Token Exchange endpoint and presents the ID Token as `subject_token`. Section 4.3.3's audience check passes because the authenticated gateway's `client_id` matches the `aud` value (or is contained in the `aud` array).

No spec changes needed; the current draft already accepts this shape. What ID-JAG could add: non-normative guidance and `azp` policy considerations.

**Pros**: standard OIDC claims, no new artifacts, current spec accommodates.

**Cons**:
- **Bearer ID Token, no PoP**: public clients can't key-bind (see [OpenID Connect Key Binding](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-key-binding-1_0.html)); any party that captures the token can present it at the gateway.
- **`azp` is discouraged outside extensions**: OIDC Core (§2) says implementations "are encouraged to not use `azp` and to ignore it when it does occur" outside specific extensions; no enforceable initiator binding.
- **No delegation scope in the ID Token**: identity assertion, not a per-invocation grant.
- **Consent granularity mismatch**: user consent is to the agent at login, not the specific gateway task.
- **IdP-side pre-config required**: not universally supported; no request-time audience selection; a new OIDC profile would be needed for cross-vendor interop.

## Option B: Identity Continuation Assertion

An identity continuation pattern where an intermediate presents a signed assertion from a Chain Authority to obtain a fresh ID-JAG for the next audience. Premise: re-subjecting across trust domains is a mint, not an attenuation.

- Note: https://notes.karlmcguinness.com/notes/identity-continuation-assertion/
- Principle: https://notes.karlmcguinness.com/notes/re-subjecting-is-a-mint-not-an-attenuation/
- Sketched draft (Appendix D covers a gateway with dynamic upstream audiences): https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-oauth-id-continuation-assertion/draft-mcguinness-oauth-id-continuation-assertion.html

**Pros**: general (arbitrary chains, dynamic audiences); no per-pair pre-configuration; works when the intermediate is credential-less at the target.

**Cons**:
- **Experimental / work-in-progress**: personal draft, not a WG document; no security analysis, no interop, no reference implementation; mechanics may change substantially.
- **New Chain Authority role**: an additional trusted issuer alongside the IdP; governance, discovery, and trust anchor setup between them are undefined.
- **Public-client entry point unsolved**: current draft assumes mutually-authenticated intermediates at the Chain Authority boundary.
- **Multi-issuer receipt trail**: continuation assertions live outside the ID-JAG; audit and revocation surface span both issuers.
- **Extra round trip**: intermediate calls the Chain Authority before the IdP exchange.
- **Overlap with `draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining`**: relationship to existing WG chaining work needs to be reconciled.

## Delegated-authority bindings

Framing the exchange output as a fresh, IdP-signed record of delegated authority (rather than a re-audienced ID Token) matches ID-JAG's design intent. Most of what you list is already there:

| Binding                        | ID-JAG today                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Subject user                   | `sub` / `sub_id`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Initiating public client       | **Gap.** Options A and B close this differently: A carries the initiator via `azp` on the subject_token (bounded by pre-configured agent-gateway trust); B binds it explicitly in the continuation assertion.                                                                                                   |
| Confidential gateway identity  | Bound implicitly via Token Exchange client authentication; not restated as a claim in the ID-JAG payload                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Requested downstream audience  | `aud` (RAS)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Actor / delegation chain       | `act` claim already defined as OPTIONAL; the *Actor Delegation Extensions* section reserves validation/authorization semantics for future profiles (see [`draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile/), *OAuth Actor Profile for Delegation*) |
| Tool / resource scope          | `scope` and/or `authorization_details` (RAR)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Policy version / decision time | `iat` gives decision time; policy version would fit as an additional claim (the spec allows "additional authentication, identity, or authorization claims valid for an ID Token")                                                                                                                               |
| Expiry / revocation context    | `exp`, `jti`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

Both directions preserve the property you're asking for: the IdP evaluates a fresh policy over `(initiator, gateway, audience, scope)` and mints an ID-JAG accordingly, rather than the gateway silently re-audiencing an inbound ID Token. Option A bounds "cross-domain minting" by requiring IdP-side pre-configuration of the agent-gateway trust; it does not hand generic minting authority to the public client. Profiling `act` semantics and defining a policy-version claim feel worth raising as separate concerns regardless of the public-client thread.

## Profile, proofs, and receipts

Adjacent layers of the same trust chain, complementary to the bindings above:

- **Actor profile** (agent description: model, version, capabilities, tool allowlist): candidate homes are nested inside RFC 8693 `act`, a separate `actor_profile` claim, or per-request inside `authorization_details`. Related work: [`draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-actor-profile/), [`draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth/), [WIMSE WG](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/wimse/about/) for workload identity.
- **Proofs** assembled before the mint: PoP ([RFC 9449 DPoP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449), [RFC 8705 mTLS](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8705), already supported); attestation ([RFC 9334 RATS architecture](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9334), [SPIFFE](https://spiffe.io/)); consent proofs; policy-version binding.
- **Receipts** of decisions: the ID-JAG is itself a receipt (signed, audience-bound, jti-tracked); the RAS-issued access token is a receipt of the RAS's authorization decision; user-consent records, where produced, live alongside. See also [`draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens/) for cross-service audit trails within a trust domain and [`draft-fletcher-transaction-token-chaining-profile`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-fletcher-transaction-token-chaining-profile/) for multi-hop chaining.

Together: `profile + proofs → policy decision → receipt`. ID-JAG plays the receipt role for the delegation step. Standardizing the profile and proof claim shapes so relying parties consume them uniformly is a separable work item worth its own discussion.

## Trade-off

Cross-client + `azp` is lighter to deploy when the gateway is pre-known and pre-configured with the IdP, but the security concerns above (bearer forwarding by a public client, unreliable `azp` binding, no delegation scope in the ID Token) constrain what it can safely be used for. ICA is more general and closes the delegation-binding gap, but is experimental, introduces a new authority role, and doesn't yet cover the public-client entry point. Not mutually exclusive: cross-client could handle the entry point, ICA the onward chains.

Feedback welcome on which deployment shape you have (single gateway pre-configured with the IdP, or something more dynamic) and whether the two-solution split matches how you're thinking about it.

@aaronpk may have some thoughts on this as well

comments.author: zekth
comments.body:
Joining this thread. The conflict @leleueri describes is one we ran into as well while integrating the ID-JAG design into a gateway, and we spent a good amount of time trying to work out a clean solution for it, so this resonates strongly. I agree with the principle @mcguinness articulated: > Forwarding the public client's ID Token to the gateway to present as its own `subject_token` is discouraged. The gateway is not the audience, and ID Tokens are not designed for cross-audience or cross-domain presentation. Section 4.3.3's audience check enforces that principle. I want to build on it with one observation: the risk this check guards against is tied specifically to **Dynamic Client Registration**. Where the IdP instead administers an explicit link between the initiating client and an authorized broker, there is a narrow, well-scoped room for an `act`-based relaxation that does not weaken the principle at all. A significant and growing class of enterprise gateway deployments create exactly that condition, because they provision the client centrally (MDM) rather than by DCR. ## The audience concern is really about unpredictable clients Presenting a user's ID Token at a party that is not its audience is dangerous because, in the open web, the presenting client is **unpredictable**. With Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591), any party can register and obtain a `client_id`. The IdP has no prior knowledge of which agent legitimately fronts which gateway, so it cannot tell a genuine broker from an attacker replaying a captured ID Token. In that world the strict `aud == client_id` check in 4.3.3 is the only guard, and any `act`/broker relaxation would mean trusting a client identity the IdP cannot vouch for. So the rule is exactly right for the DCR / open-client case. The question is whether that is the case enterprise gateways are actually in, and I do not think it is. ## Corporate deployments do not use DCR for the agent They pin the client. IT deploys the agent through MDM and pushes a **fixed, pre-registered `client_id`** to every managed instance instead of letting each install self-register. Claude Code supports this directly: `claude mcp add --client-id / --client-secret` (v2.1.30) hands every install a static `client_id` in place of per-install DCR. The result: - One `client_id` and one audience across the whole fleet, controlled by IT. - Each user still runs their own `authorization_code` + PKCE flow, so the token's `sub` (and group/role claims) is distinct per person even though `client_id` and `aud` are identical fleet-wide. - PKCE, not a shared secret, binds each authorization code to the instance that started it, so a pushed `client_secret` is only an app identifier and not the trust boundary. The initiating client's identity is now **well-known and centrally administered**. Within this trust domain, the unpredictability that motivated the strict audience check is gone: the IdP and the gateway know exactly which `client_id` a legitimate agent presents. ## Why this lets `act` relax 4.3.3 safely Here the trusted-broker `act` pattern applies with real justification. The gateway acts as a **registered broker**: a confidential client the IdP has explicitly authorized to exchange tokens on behalf of named initiating clients. It presents the user's ID Token (`aud = corp-agent`, the known MDM client) together with an `actor_token`. The IdP relaxes the `aud == client_id` requirement because: - it recognizes `corp-agent` as a pre-provisioned client it administers, not an arbitrary DCR registration; - it recognizes the gateway as a registered broker authorized for that client; - it evaluates fresh policy over `(user, corp-agent, gateway, audience, scope)`, records `corp-agent` as the client and `act = gateway` as the broker in the minted ID-JAG. The safety comes from the **link between two facts the IdP itself administers**: the initiating client (`corp-agent`) and the broker authorized to act for it. MDM is what makes the client side of that link trustworthy and fleet-scalable, but the link, not MDM alone, is the mechanism. Note this never relies on `azp`: the ID Token is addressed to `corp-agent` and was obtained by `corp-agent`, so the initiator binding comes from the administered link and is recorded in `act`, avoiding the `azp` binding OIDC Core discourages. The relaxation stays scoped to the **closed set of provisioned client_ids the enterprise controls**. The principle @mcguinness stated stays fully intact for everyone outside that set: DCR-registered and public clients still hit the strict audience check, because for them the IdP genuinely cannot vouch for the presenter. The distinction is not "brokers may replay any ID Token" but "the IdP may relax the audience check between two clients it has itself provisioned and linked." One cost to state plainly: this relaxation raises the value of a captured `corp-agent` ID Token. Under strict 4.3.3 a stolen ID Token is useless at the exchange, because its `aud` does not match the broker; once a broker may exchange it, capturing it in transit to the gateway yields upstream access for the victim. That is not a reason to avoid the relaxation, but it is exactly why key-binding the ID Token matters more here, not less (see suggestion 3 below). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant MDM as MDM / IT actor User participant Agent as Agent instance
(MDM-pinned client_id) participant IdP as Enterprise IdP participant Gateway as MCP Gateway
(registered broker) participant RAS as Resource AS
(knows Gateway) participant MCP as Upstream MCP MDM->>Agent: Provision fixed client_id=corp-agent (no DCR) User->>Agent: Initiate action Agent->>IdP: auth-code + PKCE (client_id=corp-agent) IdP-->>Agent: ID Token (aud=corp-agent, sub=user) Agent->>Gateway: Tool call + user ID Token Note over Gateway,IdP: Brokered exchange. relaxation is safe because corp-agent is well-known Gateway->>IdP: Token Exchange (subject_token=ID Token aud=corp-agent,
actor_token=gateway, audience=RAS) + gateway client auth Note right of IdP: corp-agent is MDM-provisioned, gateway is a registered broker.
Relax aud==client_id, policy over (user, corp-agent, gateway, RAS) IdP-->>Gateway: ID-JAG (sub=user, aud=RAS, client=corp-agent, act=gateway) Gateway->>RAS: jwt-bearer (assertion=ID-JAG) + resource client auth RAS-->>Gateway: Access Token (aud=MCP) Gateway->>MCP: Call + Bearer token MCP-->>Gateway: Result Gateway-->>Agent: Result ``` ## This also relaxes the MCP discovery problem There is a second payoff worth calling out, because it is the part that makes public well-known MCP servers actually workable behind a gateway. MCP authorization has the client discover each resource's Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), read `authorization_servers`, and audience-bind its token to that resource. That is fine when the client addresses a server directly. It gets messy the moment a gateway proxies a public server: - The client would have to hold both identities: the real resource identifier (e.g. GitHub's) and the proxied one the gateway exposes. RFC 9728 requires the `resource` field to equal, verbatim, the identifier used to fetch the metadata, so the proxy cannot cleanly advertise the real resource as its own. The client is left disambiguating "real vs proxied" endpoints and guessing which audience to target. Under this delegation model the client never touches any of that. Its only OAuth interaction is authenticating at the enterprise IdP as `corp-agent`, which yields an ID Token whose audience is its own `client_id` (the MDM-provisioned `corp-agent` the gateway already recognizes). It then sends that ID Token to the **gateway** with the tool call. It does not mint anything for an upstream, and it does not discover, name, or audience-bind to any resource, real or proxied. There is no mixing of real and proxied identifiers and no verbatim-`resource` conflict on the client side, because the client never performs resource discovery at all. The gateway absorbs the whole discovery burden, which is correct because it is the only party with the context to do it: per call it resolves the real upstream (its own RFC 9728 lookups or configuration), sets the right audience internally, and for public servers that do not federate the enterprise IdP it falls back to provider-native OAuth. The messy part lives in exactly one place instead of being pushed onto every client. So the delegation does two things at once: it unblocks the mint, and it collapses the client's discovery surface to a single resource. The client deals with the gateway and nothing else. ## Boundaries that still hold - **Only within the provisioned trust domain.** The relaxation is justified by MDM control of the client. Outside it (unmanaged, DCR, BYO agents) the strict 4.3.3 check must remain, exactly as @mcguinness described. - **It is a normative change, not off-the-shelf behavior.** An IdP that enforces 4.3.3 strictly will reject the brokered exchange today. This needs the spec to define the exemption and the IdP to implement it; a stock IdP does not do it now. ## What I would suggest for the spec 1. **Make the relaxation conditional on provisioned client trust.** Define the `act`/broker exemption from `aud == client_id` so it applies only when the IdP administers both the initiating client and the broker (non-DCR, pre-registered clients), with `act` recorded. Concretely, this could be a registration attribute linking an initiating client to its authorized broker(s), checked at exchange time. This keeps the audience check strict wherever the presenter is unpredictable. 2. **Acknowledge the MDM-pinned client_id shape.** A fixed, fleet-wide `client_id` with per-user `sub` is a common enterprise posture, and it is what makes a well-known initiator possible. Non-normative guidance here would help implementers reason about when the relaxation is safe. 3. **The public-client PoP question still stands.** Even a well-known client hands a bearer ID Token to the gateway; key-binding it (the direction in #85 and #113) strengthens the entry point regardless of the above. Interested in whether this framing matches how others are thinking about the enterprise case, and glad to dig into any of it further.

comments.author: leleueri
comments.body:
Option B proposed by @mcguinness seems to be the most generic approach, although it might be the most complex to implement.

On the other hand, @zekth's solution feels more pragmatic and straightforward to roll out with minimal changes to the specification. However, forwarding an `id_token` to a third party (even a trusted one) feels counter-intuitive and could introduce security or privacy risks, as the `id_token` will likely contain much broader user information than what is strictly required. 

That said, this risk is likely mitigated if we assume an enterprise context where the Gateway and the IdP are operated by the same legal entity. Furthermore, if the IdP is configured to include the Gateway as a valid audience (`aud`) alongside the agent client, it is probably acceptable (happy to be contradicted here).

In any case, introducing sender-binding / key-binding for public clients seems like a solid addition to strengthen security around this `id_token` exchange.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Thanks @zekth for the reply, this is super helpful. TL;DR: it sounds like your suggestion is to implement the cross-client identity pattern using `actor_token` instead of `azp`. If I understand your comment correctly, you are proposing two things:

1. a new profile for cross-client identity at the Token Exchange layer, and
2. a deployment profile for a broker.

I went ahead and sketched out what these two might look like:

- [Token Exchange Profile for Cross-Client Delegation](https://gist.github.com/mcguinness/aa44d94a0ed45827985e7f3ade17852c#file-token-exchange-cross-client-delegation-sketch-md): generic mechanism (CCDR, `actor_token`, `may_act`, `act` claim construction).
- [ID-JAG Enterprise Broker Deployment Pattern](https://gist.github.com/mcguinness/aa44d94a0ed45827985e7f3ade17852c#file-id-jag-broker-profile-md): informative deployment pattern applying the generic profile to the enterprise MDM + gateway shape.

**Disclaimer**: these are just sketches, generated with AI assistance, and may not be complete or fully consistent. Sharing to see if the shape aligns with what you had in mind.

Two framing questions worth calling out:

- **Cross-client as its own extension vs. coupled to ID-JAG.** The generic profile applies to any Token Exchange scenario, not just ID-JAG. Worth deciding whether cross-client identity is useful enough on its own to warrant a standalone OAuth WG extension that ID-JAG references, or whether it should live inside the ID-JAG spec directly. My instinct is standalone.
- **Deployment pattern as informational.** I would not expect the deployment pattern to live in the ID-JAG spec itself. It reads more like an informational companion document for implementers targeting the enterprise gateway shape.

Let me know if this is aligned with what your comment was after.

comments.author: zekth
comments.body:
Happy to help @mcguinness. So far so good, and it also frames one important thing, which is the consent part of the flow.

One other thing that came to mind: the Gateway should advertise that it expects an `id_token` as the `subject_token_type` for this delegation pattern. This could be exposed via the AS's `.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` metadata, in a new property such as `authorization_grant_profiles_supported`.

Concretely, this would let a Gateway (or any confidential client acting as an intermediary) discover ahead of time whether the IdP supports this profile at all, rather than attempting a Token Exchange call and failing. It also gives us a clean extension point to signal support for the actor-token / identity-chaining pattern raised in point 1 above. An AS could advertise which `subject_token_type` / `actor_token_type` combinations it's willing to accept for a given profile, so a Gateway can determine up front whether "exchange this Agent-issued ID Token on behalf of the Gateway" is even a supported combination for that IdP, instead of discovering it only through a runtime rejection.

There's a symmetric problem on the client side too: the Agent itself needs a way to discover which token kind it should be sending to the Gateway in the first place (an `id_token`, an access token scoped to the Gateway, or something else), rather than that being a hardcoded assumption baked into the client. Without that discovery step, every Agent implementation has to guess or be manually configured, which doesn't scale well across different Gateway deployments.

Curious what others think: does it make more sense as a new top-level metadata property, or as an extension to the existing `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` / grant-types metadata we already have? And should client-facing discovery (what to send to the Gateway) and AS-facing discovery (what the Gateway can exchange) be expressed through the same mechanism, or kept separate since they serve different actors in the flow?

comments.author: kierandotai
comments.body:
I want to add one dimension I don't think any of the options have covered. The bindings discussion already covers per-artifact expiry and revocation: exp and jti in @mcguinness's table, and the "expiry and revocation context" @0xbrainkid listed. That is revocation of a single ID-JAG. It is not the same as revocation propagation across an established chain, which none of the options addresses: when authority is revoked at one point in a delegation chain, is authority already derived downstream from it invalidated, and over what window?

I raise it as an implementer. We run a broker in the gateway seat this issue describes. Not an ID-JAG deployment (our upstreams don't redeem IdP-minted assertions), but the same recorded-chain shape, minting a fresh signed artifact per hop with the ancestor bound in. We found that recording the chain and enforcing it are different things. Revocation gets checked at the hop where a credential is presented; unless every hop re-validates the full ancestor lineage, a revoked ancestor keeps authorizing descendants that were minted before the revocation. Revoking the root of a chain did not stop the chain. It is invisible at depth one and surfaces only at depth two or more, which is the agent-behind-agent-behind-gateway case this topology produces.

Where it bites in the options on the table:

The act / may_act cross-client delegation being sketched binds the initiator and broker into the minted ID-JAG at mint time. That is a point-in-time record. If the initiating client is later deprovisioned, or the broker's authorization to act for it is withdrawn, nothing in a mint-time act binding stops a chain that was already minted from being extended, unless the profile requires the status of every ancestor to be checked at each subsequent mint. That feels like it belongs in the profile being sketched here, not left to implementations to discover.
It sharpens @zekth's own caveat about a captured corp-agent ID Token. If deprovisioning the initiating corp-agent does not propagate to chains already derived from it, the window on a captured-token or deprovisioned-agent compromise is bounded by artifact exp, not by revocation, which is a weaker guarantee than the enterprise-broker framing suggests.

Suggestion: whichever mechanism lands, state whether ancestor revocation must propagate to existing chains and over what window, with the default that an intermediary-issued artifact carrying no verifiable ancestor lineage cannot propagate ancestor revocation and should therefore be treated as valid only to its own exp.

In the single-IdP topology here this is tractable, because one authority issues every hop and can check each ancestor's status at mint. It stops being free once the hops span organizations, which is the cold-start gap on the use-cases side (UC5 and the cross-organizational companion case). Same problem, two hops apart.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Thanks @kierandotai and @zekth. Both points really landed and are captured in the updated [gist](https://gist.github.com/mcguinness/aa44d94a0ed45827985e7f3ade17852c).

To keep this thread focused: this issue isn't the right venue for continuing to resolve design details on the sketches. If either shape (Cross-Client Delegation profile, Enterprise Broker deployment pattern) has enough interest to move forward, they need to become I-D drafts with authors willing to shepherd them. Detailed design review is best done against those I-Ds once they exist.

My goal in sketching these was really to get signal on whether this belongs as a change to ID-JAG or its own profile. Based on the discussion here, I'm convinced it's the latter. Recommendation: move to their own I-D drafts. Happy to hand off notes.

comments.author: gffletch

issues.title: Add rationale for `subject_token` type selection (function vs OAuth token type)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

Readers frequently ask why they can't use an access token as `subject_token`. The current parameter definition (Section 4.3) enumerates supported types (ID Token, SAML 2.0 Assertion, Refresh Token) but does not explain the underlying design principle: token selection is by function at the IdP Authorization Server, not by OAuth token type. The exclusion rationale needs to be documented explicitly.

## Proposal

Add a new subsection `### Subject Token Type Selection` to the Token Exchange section (§4.3), after the parameter definitions and before Processing Rules.

## Draft text

> ID-JAG selects `subject_token` by function at the IdP Authorization Server, not by OAuth token type:
>
> * **Identity Assertion**: conveys the authenticated subject directly (ID Token, SAML 2.0 assertion).
> * **Identity Continuity**: lets the IdP Authorization Server issue a fresh identity assertion from an existing authorization grant (Refresh Token).
> * **Resource Authorization**: authorizes access to a protected resource (access token).
>
> This profile supports identity assertion and identity continuity credentials.
>
> An access token may carry identity claims ([RFC 9068 §2.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068.html#name-identity-claims)) and authentication context claims such as `auth_time`, `acr`, and `amr` ([RFC 9068 §2.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068.html#name-authentication-information-)). The RFC permits both so that resource servers can consume them directly for their own authorization decisions, without introspection or UserInfo round-trips, particularly in same-entity / same-solution scenarios such as first-party clients invoking their own backend API. These claims are for resource-server-side consumption, not for identity assertion to a third party. An access token is not an identity assertion for the client, and its primary contract is authorization to a resource. OIDC introduced the ID Token because OAuth access tokens were intentionally not suitable as a portable authentication artifact.
>
> The exclusion applies in three scenarios:
>
> **IdP-issued access tokens.** The token was issued for presentation to a specific protected resource (typically identified by an `aud` claim), not for identity brokering. When encrypted for that resource, the token may not be decryptable by the client or other parties, reinforcing that it was constructed for that resource. Using it as a `subject_token` expands the credential's purpose beyond the authorization context it was issued for, regardless of the Authorization Server's ability to introspect. **UserInfo access tokens are excluded on the same grounds**: they authorize access to an identity resource but remain resource authorization credentials, and the ID Token already covers identity assertion to the client.
>
> **IdP-issued access tokens for a first-party resource acting as an ID-JAG client.** The resource is same-entity with the IdP, so the RFC 9068 rationale for including these claims most naturally applies. The exclusion still holds. The claims exist for the resource's own authorization decisions, not to be brokered onward. When such a resource needs to obtain an ID-JAG on behalf of a user, the base profile assumes an identity assertion or identity continuity credential is available. Bridging from an access-token-only starting point is a separable design question; a complementary profile would need to define how identity and authentication claims are extracted from the access token, how policy is re-evaluated for the ID-JAG audience, and how the access token's scope and consent align with the ID-JAG's requested authorization.
>
> **Externally-issued access tokens with the IdP as intended recipient.** Accepting these as identity-bearing input would establish a federation model in which the external issuer authorizes identity brokering through the IdP Authorization Server. That is a substantive federation trust decision beyond the base ID-JAG profile.
>
> Restricting identity exchange to identity assertion and identity continuity credentials keeps identity establishment and resource authorization separate, which is what lets IdP and Resource Authorization Server implementations converge on interoperable identity semantics without coupling to any specific access-token structure or introspection contract.

Happy to open a PR if the direction lands.

issues.title: Constraints on `resource` parameter in Token Exchange
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
If a Resource AS defines 3 `resource` values: `A`, `B`, and `C`, what are the expectations for the values a client can include in the `resource` parameters in Token Exchange?

My assumption is the client would be able to ask for any combination of the 3:

* `A`
* `B`
* `A`, `B`
* `B`, `C`
* `A`, `C`
* `A`, `B`, `C`

and if the client includes one that is not defined `D`, that is an error.

This isn't explicit in Token Exchange:

> An authorization server can use the invalid_target error code, defined in [Section 2.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8693/#ErrorResponse), to inform a client that it requested access to too many target services simultaneously.

but since this has come up in implementation discussions of this spec, we should probably include some guidance. Ideally normative language, but at least something informative.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Good catch, I agree with your assumption.  

I think it makes sense to adopt `invalid_target` from [RFC 8707
Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707.html) in this spec for when the client asks for a resource outside of the allowed set.   We also need to define behavior for the IdP AS  when it only accepts a subset of the requested resources or provides a default resource.  This was the premise in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-resource-token-resp/ as the security gap in RFC 8707.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Related to #122. Aaron's scenario there depends on the IdP not enforcing a `resource` parameter, which is exactly the gap this issue closes. The response-confirmation piece is already specified in [draft-mcguinness-oauth-resource-token-resp](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-resource-token-resp/) (cited in my earlier comment); ID-JAG can either reference it normatively or inline the minimum needed (`invalid_target`, response `resource` confirmation) and cite it as informative. Either resolution lets #122's security consideration cite the same source and present the client-side `iss` check and the IdP-side `resource` check as a pair.

issues.title: Carry an optional client metadata digest so the IdP can vouch for the client's CIMD (JIT provisioning at the RAS)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

ID-JAG lets an IdP that both domains already trust assert a user's identity and a client's delegated authorization to a Resource Authorization Server (RAS). That trust gives the RAS a strong reason to believe the user and the delegation. It says nothing about the *client's metadata*: its name, `redirect_uris`, key material, and other registration attributes. The draft assumes the client is "already known" to the RAS, established out of band or via a client metadata document, and #113 notes that even the client's `client_id` at the boundary needs a normative identification story.

Where the client is identified by a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) URL, this leaves an open question the CIMD trust model does not itself answer: *who reviewed and vouches for this client's metadata?* CIMD anchors that the metadata authentically came from whoever controls the URL. It does not tell the RAS that a trusted party evaluated that metadata. In the ID-JAG deployment model the RAS already trusts exactly such a party: the IdP.

## Solution sketch

Let the IdP bind a digest of the client's CIMD document into the assertion it already signs, so the RAS can trust the client's metadata on the IdP's signature and provision the client just in time. Details are for the working group to choose:

- Define an OPTIONAL `cimd_digest` claim carried in the ID-JAG, or established through the ID Token to ID-JAG chain. Its value is the unpadded base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash ([RFC 6234](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6234.html)) of the client's retrieved CIMD representation body, taken after any content coding is removed and with no transcoding or normalization, so no JSON canonicalization is involved. Other drafts in the working group have defined this same `cimd_digest` binding; reusing the claim and its computation keeps it interoperable.
- The `client_id` is the CIMD URL, consistent with CIMD and with the client-identification gap #113 raises.
- The IdP is already relying on this document. When the client is CIMD-identified at the IdP, the IdP has already fetched and trusted the same CIMD, including its keys and `redirect_uris`, to authenticate the client and issue the ID Token and refresh token that underlie the identity assertion. Signing a `cimd_digest` attests a document the IdP already consumed and trusted for this exchange; it is the digest of what the IdP saw, not a new review it must run. The keys #113 relies on to key-bind the ID Token are the same keys carried in that vouched CIMD.
- On redemption, a RAS that does not already know the client MAY provision it just in time: fetch the CIMD URL, verify the document's `client_id` equals the URL, recompute the digest, and compare it to the IdP-asserted `cimd_digest`. On a match, it provisions a client from that metadata and trusts it because the IdP it already trusts signed over that exact snapshot.
- If the RAS must complete anything asynchronously first, for example a first-sighting review of a client it has never seen, it can defer the token response and let the client poll rather than defining new async machinery here. [Deferred Token Response](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response-00.html) already defines this at the token endpoint: the server answers with `authorization_pending`, a `deferral_code`, and a polling interval, and the client polls a deferred grant until the token is ready. Because redeeming an ID-JAG is itself a token-endpoint exchange, it composes directly, with no addition to this draft.

The effect is that an ID-JAG carrying `cimd_digest` acts, for the client's metadata, almost like a software statement over the CIMD: the IdP signs over the digest, and the RAS gets trusted metadata plus a just-in-time client without a separate registration call or a separate issuer to configure.

## Benefits

- **Answers "who vouches for the client's metadata" inside the existing trust model.** The RAS already trusts the IdP for SSO and subject resolution; this lets the same trust cover the client's metadata, with no new issuer relationship to establish.
- **Just-in-time provisioning of unknown clients.** A RAS can accept a client it has never registered, cross-domain, because the metadata arrives vouched for by the IdP and bound by digest to a CIMD the RAS can fetch and verify.
- **Minimal, and built on existing reliance.** One optional claim on a JWT the IdP already issues, over a CIMD the IdP already fetched and trusted to issue the ID Token and refresh token. No new endpoint, artifact, or round trip, and no new review obligation for the CIMD-identified case.
- **Composes** with CIMD (`client_id` = URL, digest binds the reviewed snapshot) and with [Deferred Token Response](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response-00.html) for any asynchronous completion at the RAS.
- **Reinforces #113.** That issue removes the confidential-client requirement when the client is key-bound and flags that the `client_id` still needs a normative identity. A CIMD URL vouched for by `cimd_digest` gives that identity a trusted, fetchable, IdP-attested form. Together, a key-bound public client (#113) whose CIMD the IdP vouches for (this issue) can be provisioned at the RAS with both authenticated key binding and trusted metadata.

## Tradeoffs

- **The IdP vouches for client metadata, not just user identity.** Where the client is CIMD-identified this formalizes reliance the IdP already had, but the assurance is still bounded by the IdP's process: a light "we recognize this client" is weaker than a real review, and the RAS can conclude only what the IdP actually did. The spec should name any review beyond the IdP's existing client authentication as deployment policy.
- **It couples a client-metadata attestation onto a user-authorization grant.** Some deployments may prefer to keep "who is the user" and "what is the client software" in separate artifacts. A standalone establishment artifact is the better fit when there is no user in the loop or no shared IdP, which is out of scope here and is where other drafts' trust binding applies. This proposal is specifically for the case ID-JAG already serves.
- **Digest-change semantics need a rule.** The digest is over the whole document, so a benign change (a fixed typo) and a material one (a new redirect URI) both break it. The draft would need to say whether a mismatch is a hard failure or a policy input, ideally distinguishing changes to attested versus unattested metadata.
- **Trust must anchor to the configured IdP, not the CIMD's own keys.** Standard issuer-trust discipline; the cross-domain client ID handling caution in the draft and #113 applies.

## Relation to #113

#113 is about *authentication assurance*: relaxing the confidential-client requirement when the ID Token or ID-JAG is key-bound. This issue is about *metadata trust and provisioning*: letting the IdP vouch for the client's CIMD so the RAS can trust and JIT-provision it. They are independent but complementary and strongest together: #113 lets the client be public and key-bound; this lets the RAS know and trust that client's metadata without prior registration. #113 also leaves open how the `client_id` is identified in the public-client case, and a CIMD URL carried with `cimd_digest` is a concrete answer.

## Asking for

Feedback on whether this belongs in the base spec or a profile, whether `cimd_digest` should ride the ID-JAG or be established in the ID Token chain, and how strict RAS-side digest-mismatch handling should be. If the direction has interest, I am happy to work the processing rules (digest computation, JIT-provisioning validation, mismatch policy) into a PR.

issues.title: add security consideration about the extra importance of validating the AS issuer URL
issues.author: aaronpk
issues.body:
RFC8414 [already includes](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8414#section-3.3) language about validating that the `iss` in the AS metadata matches the URL it was fetched from. However, it's extra important to validate that in the context of this spec, since more things are happening without user interaction.

We should add a new security consideration section that discusses the validation required and the reason for doing so.

Below is a scenario that can trivially lead to account takeovers if the validation step is not done by the client.

---

The attacker's hosts an MCP server at `https://mcp.attacker.com/`, and its Protected Resource Metadata points to the attacker's AS `https://auth.attacker.com/`

The attacker hosts AS metadata at `https://auth.attacker.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` with the following contents:

```
{
  "iss": "https://auth.example.com/",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://auth.attacker.com/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://auth.attacker.com/token",
  ...
}
```

This is invalid according to RFC8414 because the `iss` value in this metadata doesn't match the URL it was requested from. However if the client continues, it would make a request for an ID-JAG with the issuer of a real MCP server `https://auth.example.com/`.

The attack occurs starting with getting a user to connect the malicious MCP server.

Without a `resource` parameter, the IDP wouldn't be able to tell that the request for the ID-JAG with `iss=https://auth.example.com` is starting from a malicious MCP server, so the IDP would issue an ID-JAG with the audience of `https://auth.example.com`. At that point, the client sends the ID-JAG to the attacker's token endpoint, and the attacker can forward it on to the real MCP AS and get the access token for the real MCP server.

---

This is not a new attack, the same thing is possible in an interactive OAuth flow. But I think it's worth reminding people about again here because of how subtle this kind of thing can be.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Related to #120. The attack here leans on the absence of a validated `resource` parameter ("Without a `resource` parameter, the IDP wouldn't be able to tell..."), which is what #120 is scoped to constrain.

Not a duplicate; they compose:

- **#122**: client-side obligation to validate AS metadata `iss` matches the URL it was fetched from (RFC 8414 §3.3), landing as a new security consideration.
- **#120**: server-side normative behavior for the `resource` parameter (`invalid_target` on out-of-set, partial-accept, default resource) plus response confirmation. The behavior is already specified in [draft-mcguinness-oauth-resource-token-resp](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-resource-token-resp/); ID-JAG can either normatively reference it, or inline the minimum needed (`invalid_target`, response `resource` confirmation) and cite it as informative.

Either way, the security consideration here should cross-reference #120 so the client-side `iss` check and the IdP-side `resource` check read as a pair rather than as alternatives.

comments.author: KevinLuo2000
comments.body:
This is a good call-out. The authenticity of AS metadata (and in fact of all metadata documents in OAuth) MUST be strictly validated; failing to do so would greatly impact the security of _downstream specs_ dependent on them, yet their implementers may overlook such validation. For example, IMO it's a bit unfortunate that RFC9207 did not restate RFC8414 Section 3.3. 

But at least in the MCP world, I added a [note](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/2468#discussion_r3139014444) on this in the MCP iss validation PR, and it now stands in the [AS metadata discovery section](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization/authorization-server-discovery#authorization-server-metadata-discovery) in the MCP authorization spec, independent of the mix-up defense (and hopefully a reminder to ID-JAG/Enterprise-Managed Auth implementers as well?).

Each relationship is typically represented by independent client registrations between each party. comments.body:
> It's great that we agree that context is required to make the authorization decision and decide the contents of the ID-JAG. I believe much of the context won't be with the IdP, and an Enterprise Authorization Server can leverage such dynamic context in order to determine the content and the decision to issue the ID-JAG.

The concern I attempted to articulate is with identity chaining.   Using an access token as a way to chain an interactive session from the IdP issuer to the EAS  issuer is lossy that wasn't there when the IdP was providing the EAS role .  Its 3 different trust domains instead of 2.  The access token from the IdP to the EAS has no resource context as the IdP only knows a client is requesting an Access Token  to the EAS but nothing else.  It can't enforce its part of the zero-trust policy  (e.g A client can only act as an enterprise user to a managed resource if only the user signed-in in from a managed device to a managed app with phishing resistant mfa).  

IdPs MAY implement Authorization in addition to Authentication concerns, IdPs MAY have shared signals, identify fabric integrations, and device trust context, and IdPs MAY even leverage an external authorization policy decision point.   The argument I was highlighting is that customers will already need to solve these integration challenges (IGA, PAM, ISPM, Externalized Policy, Device Trust, Shared Signals, etc) with best of breed components with their IdP.  The IdP doesn't need to own all the roles but these other roles don't need to be the identity issuer for a federated OAuth 2.0 authorization grant to achieve the outcome.   

If we want to remove all the constraints of identity chaining the original draft imposed and solve for BYO OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server as the EAS then I think the simpler solution is to just allow the Resource Authorization Server to accept a JWT Access Token issued by any trusted Authorization Server just as long as the audience of token is the Resource AS issuer or token endpoint and stop trying to leverage a special profile of JWT Authorization Grant.

comments.author: aaronpk
comments.body:
The more I think about this, it's specifically the coupling of the ID Token Issuer and ID-JAG issuer that make this draft unique and make it interoperable. 

Prior to this extension, we've had the "Identity and Authorization Chaining" draft in the OAuth working group for 2 years. That draft doesn't prescribe whether the input token is an ID token or access token (though kind of assumes it will be an access token), and also doesn't prescribe any relationship between the issuer of the input token and the issuer of the cross-domain token.

In other words, you can already do this with the "Identity and Authorization Chaining" draft today, or you can do this by just configuring the resource AS to trust an arbitrary JWT issuer like Karl described. You don't need this draft in order to do that.

This draft is useful specifically or the case where ID tokens are used, and where the ID token issuer *is* where the policies for cross-app access live.

reviews.author: mcguinness
reviews.body:
We should define the pros and cons of this approach.  Here are some I can think of

Pro
- IdP doesn't have to natively support ID-JAG enabling adoption  of ID-JAG outside of IdP as the Resource AS can trust different issuers
- Another enterprise system can provide an authorization capability enabling best of breed for enterprise
- Resource AS could trust multiple ID-JAG issuers for the Enterprise without complicating or changing IdP configuration for SSO

Con
- Introduces need to explain and manage/control how both issuers are part of the same trust domain and this doesn't introduce a 3rd trust domain for identity chaining.  The EAS can effectively perform an on-behalf-of for an IdP identity for a downstream resource without the IdP knowing what resource (no constrained delegation).
- More complicated discovery for Client to know how to get an ID-JAG
- Resource AS may need to support more complex claims mapping that could add more security surface area to attack.  It can't assume its the IdP and keep same account resolution logic used for SSO (e.g different issuers for example).
- More ambiguity on how this is different than Vanilla JWT Authorization Grant
- Exchanging an Access Token for an ID-JAG that looks like an Access Token just with different type for yet another Access Token adds cognitive overhead and will create confusion on why not just use the original Access Token as grant and bypass all the additional layers of abstraction.  The audience of an access token for a resource indicator request could be the EAS or the Resource AS for example.
- Introduces need to profile the Access Token for Token Exchange interoperability with Enterprise AS
- Access Token for Token Exchange may not contain necessary authentication context to make an authorization decision (e.g zero-trust) that was previously in IdP

Yes but also confidence that the user identity is consistent across tokens and that doesnt need to be verified...how is the user identity correlated across Idps?

My understanding of what @mcguinness is pointing out here, is that there are now two different issuers issuing tokens for "federation" into domain B.   For example, if SSO is being performed from domain A to domain B, an ID token would be issued such as:

```
{
   iss: "idp.a.example"
   sub: "501"
   aud: "client-domain-b"
}
```

Domain B consumes this ID token, creating a user record associated with `iss+sub`.

Now, with the split proposed here, domain B may receive an ID-JAG as follows:

```
{
  iss: "eas.a.example"
  sub: "501"
  aud: "as.b.example"
}
```

The intent here is that the same user (ID: 501) is being asserted.   However, the `iss+sub` is _different_ because the issuer is now different.  In order to safely map the user to the same account, domain B would have to have some out-of-band knowledge that the IDP and EAS represent the same domain, despite being separate issuers.

```suggestion
The `cnf` (confirmation) claim, as defined in {{RFC7800}}, is used to bind a public key to a JWT. When an ID-JAG contains a `cnf` claim with a `jkt` property as defined in {{RFC9449}}, it indicates that the ID-JAG is bound to that specific key (identified by its JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint), and proof of possession of the corresponding private key MUST be demonstrated when using the ID-JAG.
```

```suggestion
2. This enables the Resource Authorization Server to validate the key binding for the ID-JAG using simple string comparison of the JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint.
```

```suggestion
3. The token exchange response does not explicitly indicate whether key binding was successfully performed by the IdP.  The `token_type` response parameter for an ID-JAG is always `N_A` per {{Section 2.2.1 of RFC8693}}. The client SHOULD inspect the ID-JAG to determine if a `cnf` claim is present and whether it represents the same key as the DPoP proof.  This enables the client to detect if the IdP successfully processed the DPoP proof in the token exchange request and bound the issued ID-JAG, preventing the IdP from silently ignoring the DPoP proof and mitigating downgrade attacks.
```

pulls.title: Broadened the draft’s framing of Enterprise IdP to apply to more deployment scenarios
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Broaden the draft’s framing from “enterprise IdP” to the more precise trust model the protocol actually depends on: the IdP Authorization Server the downstream Resource Authorization Server already trusts for SSO and subject resolution.

This update keeps the protocol semantics intact while making the document align better with the CIAM and agentic examples already in the draft. The revised text consistently clarifies that the Resource Authorization Server still applies its own local policy and issues its own access tokens; ID-JAG changes the grant path, not resource ownership or token issuance authority.

It also tightens the cross-domain guidance for multi-hop deployments. The draft now says an ID-JAG is specific to the issuer-to-RAS trust relationship identified by `aud`, and the same ID-JAG must not be reused as the authorization grant for a different downstream Resource Authorization Server. Later hops may use newly issued ID-JAGs or other mechanisms.

Key edits:
- Update abstract, introduction, roles, and overview to describe the trusted-IdP model instead of enterprise-only framing.
- Preserve existing consent/policy semantics by clarifying that the RAS does not need to obtain user consent directly again at the token exchange step.
- Generalize use-case framing so enterprise remains a primary example, but not the only valid deployment model.
- Refresh CIAM and AI agent text to match the same trust-boundary language.

No protocol flow changes were introduced beyond clarifying the scope of ID-JAG reuse in downstream multi-hop scenarios.

comments.body:
What does the phrase `subject resolution` mean exactly? Is subject resolution something that the IDP does, or does the IDP provide inputs that are then trusted for the RAS to perform subject resolution itself. I _think_ it means the latter, but I'm not sure. From what I can see that exact phrase hasn't been used in [OAuth](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/search/?q=%22subject%20resolution%22) before. Other examples from [FHIR](https://build.fhir.org/ig/jmandel/smart-permission-tickets-wip/) describe subject resolution as something that the RP does, not the issuer.

Would `subject assertion` or `identity assertion` make more sense?

`Subject resolution` is the step where a  RP or Resource Authorization Server takes an asserted identity and determines which local subject it corresponds to.

In practice, that means mapping incoming identity data like:
- `sub`
- issuer
- email
- tenant context
- federation identifiers

to the local thing the service actually authorizes, such as:
- a user record
- an account
- a tenant member
- a service principal

Why it matters:
authentication says “this assertion is valid.”  
subject resolution says “which local identity is this, here?”  

Without subject resolution, the service cannot safely apply local authorization.

Its a pretty standard IAM term, but probably worth adding a definition to the spec as I'm sure others will have same question as you.

I think the spec in general is missing term definitions (not just roles) as we are using of lot IAM concepts in this spec as we are building on identity assertions.  I think it makes sense to have that a separate PR that adds common terms including subject resolution as well as others.

Yeah, subject resolution as a thing the resource authorization server does makes sense to me. I initially interpreted the phrasing as if the resource authorization server trusts the IdP to do subject resolution itself.

> Its a pretty standard IAM term

is it?
Attempt to solve that with https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/pull/86

Adding some term definitions is useful but I don't think it's even needed in the context of this text in the abstract. 
```suggestion
This specification provides a mechanism for an application to use an identity assertion to obtain an access token for a third-party API by coordinating through an identity provider that the downstream Resource Authorization Server already trusts for single sign-on (SSO), using Token Exchange {{RFC8693}} and JWT Profile for OAuth 2.0 Authorization Grants {{RFC7523}}.
```

I'd suggest “Identity layer” is too vague and overloaded for use in this kind of context. Also SSO doesn't really enable the enforcement of policy by the “Identity layer” operator at these applications.

```suggestion
In many deployments, applications are configured for single sign-on to a common identity provider (IdP) using OpenID Connect or SAML. This enables users to access multiple applications using a single account at the IdP, and enables the operator of that IdP to manage which users can access which applications and enforce policy for access to those applications. Enterprise workforce identity providers are one common example, but the same trust pattern can also arise in customer identity, platform identity, and other federated application ecosystems.
```

pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Resource Authorization Servers configured with SAML SSO cannot always map the JWT-style `sub` claim to a SAML NameID. This adds an optional `sub_id` claim carrying a SAML NameID in the SSO subject namespace, so the RAS can resolve users by SAML NameID without forcing `sub` and the SAML NameID to be the same value.

- Add `sub_id` claim referencing RFC 9493
- Define the `saml-nameid` Subject Identifier Format (required: `issuer`,
  `nameid`; optional: `nameid_format`, `name_qualifier`, `sp_name_qualifier`,
  `sp_provided_id`) with reference to SAML 2.0 (OASIS.saml-core-2.0-os)
- Add processing rules for the IdP (faithful derivation, same-subject
  invariant) and the RAS (tuple-based resolution, `invalid_grant` on
  missing/malformed `sub_id` when required)
- Add Security Considerations: Subject Identifier Trust (don't use
  `sub_id.issuer` to establish ID-JAG issuer trust) and Subject Identifier
  Disclosure (minimize identifiers visible to the Client)
- Register `saml-nameid` in the IANA Security Event Identifier Formats
  registry
- Soften the `sub` claim text to allow different subject namespaces
  between the ID-JAG issuer and SSO, while requiring `sub` and `sub_id`
  to identify the same End-User when both are present
- Rename the existing SAML 2.0 section to "SAML 2.0 Subject Token
  Interoperability" so it scopes only to protocol transition

pulls.title: Clarify subjects whose claims the ID-JAG conveys
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Summary

Clarifies which subjects' claims appear in an ID-JAG and how the IdP populates them, without changing normative behavior.

- Names the three subjects: End-User (`sub`), OAuth client (`client_id`), and optional actor (`act`).
- Anchors audience-scoped claim population to the same model IdPs already use for ID Tokens and SAML Assertions issued to the target Resource Authorization Server.
- Preserves the prior text's OpenID Core reference and the "Identity Assertion plus authorization delegation" framing as the closing sentence.

## Motivation

Implementer feedback indicated the previous text (`The ID-JAG may contain additional authentication, identity, or authorization claims...`) didn't make the implicit claim model obvious. In particular, audience-scoped authorization claims about the End-User (such as roles or entitlements at the target application) are first-class ID-JAG content. Naming the subjects explicitly and pointing to the existing IdP pattern resolves that without introducing new normative requirements or new claim shapes.

## Test plan
